subtopic: CONDITIONS GOVERNING TEN-YEAR EXTENSION OP BANK CHARTERS

speechtext:
Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance) moved the second reading of Bill No. 91, respecting banks and banking.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is not necessary for me to stress the importance of this bill to which the house is npw asked to give second reading. It is a bill which extends the charters of the ten commercial or so-called "chartered" banks for another ten years, specifies the types of business which these banks can carry on, and prescribes the regulations and the controls governing the conduct of their operations. These regulations and controls which are probably more comprehensive and in most respects more restrictive than are to be found in the banking laws of any other democratic country, are the product of six decennial revisions by the parliament of Canada of the first banking legislation of a general character passed in the Dominion of Canada, the Bank Act of 1871. That act in turn was the product of a rich background of a half-century's practical experience with, and legislative regulation of, a banking system which had been transplanted from Scotland and adapted to the special needs of the British colonies in North America.
The wisdom of this device of decennial revision of our banking legislation is, I think, obvious. It provides regular opportunities,
Bank Act-Mr. Ilsley

at reasonable intervals, for a full-dress review of the efficiency with which the banks are serving the needs of the public and for making such amendments to the law as changing conditions seem to require. The sense of responsibility with which parliament has acted in these periodic inquests has been commented upon by foreign observers. Breckenridge, for instance, in his history of the Canadian banking system, was impressed with the natural growth or evolution of our banking system. In his concluding paragraph he had this to say:
One of the strongest contrasts which this whole record presents to such a history of banking as that of the United States, is in the continuity of the progress. There has been no recurring struggle to establish a great government bank, no epidemic of wild-cat banking, no rejection of one system for experiment with another. A certain continuity, without doubt, can be discovered in the history of any banking system. Men do not wholly break with the past or build on foundations entirely new. But down to the present day Canadians have always held to the plan on which were framed the statutes governing their first banks. Additions have been made, new safeguards against public loss introduced, limits restraining corporate activity have been narrowed in some parts and widened in others, a few arrangements for the advantage of the government have been attached, but never has there been a successful attempt to tear down the fair work of the first builders and out of the ruins construct anew. When defects have appeared in its structure, Canadians have not forthwith condemned the heritage of the past, and petulantly, illogically swept it away to make room for some new, untried affair, arranged on different lines; after study of the trouble they have endeavoured by some slight strengthening, some little alteration, to keep and enhance the certain benefits of what they already possessed.
In an earlier passage, he made this interesting comment:
In Canada, as in Scotland, the history of banking records singularly few frauds upon the currency, and, so far as their creditors were concerned, the losses inflicted by insolvent bankers have been remarkably slight. In order to reform the system, it never became necessary to maim it; in neither country has banking developed the abuses that,

The present revision comes at a significant and appropriate time. We look forward to a decade which will include at least a number of years of transition from a war to a peace economy, years of readjustment and reconstruction, and years in which we are determined that this young country shall make great strides to bigger and better things. That prospect, it is obvious, will require not only an efficient but a strong and flexible banking system. In 1944, also, we can look back,

with some perspective, to the period of the early thirties, a period of widespread distress and general frustration as a result of which the banking system, like other economic institutions and most political institutions, became the target of constant and sometimes bitter attack.
It was perhaps only natural that this should be the case. Human nature tends to over-simplify and one of the easiest oversimplifications is to blame a major depression on the lack of credit. Certainly it might seem to the manufacturer who had to close down his business, say, in 1932, that the cause of his failure was the refusal of his bank to give him unlimited credit, but there were thousands of bankers in the United States in that year who could have explained what would, and did, happen to the banks which left their credits outstanding. The banks, of course, were not blameless, either in respect of the policies they followed in the boom years of the late twenties, policies which involved the granting of too much rather than too little credit, nor in the policies they followed with the onset of depression when faced with the necessity of saving their own institutions they may have aggravated the deflationary process which the antecedent inflationary boom had made inevitable.
But there are two points which I wish to make in this connection.
In the first place it is a travesty of economic interpretation to place responsibility for the great depression upon the Canadian banking system. The world-wide character of the depression and of the fall in prices which accompanied it should be sufficient proof of the absurdity of such a contention. It would probably take a volume to give a clear and satisfying explanation of the causes of this depression, which was unprecedented in its severity, its coverage and its persistence. Its causes were not solely, perhaps not even primarily, financial or monetary, but economic and political as well. It had its roots in the maladjustments in the world economy produced by the first world war and particularly in the wholesale use of inflationary methods for financing that war by all or nearly all the belligerent countries. The consequences of that inflationary finance, in the form of distorted price levels, unbalanced economies, unstable currencies, political instability and resurgence of economic nationalism, posed for the world a series of economic and political problems of difficulty almost beyond the wit of man to solve. Certainly the statesmanship of the leading nations in the twenties showed neither the courage nor the imagination to solve them. On the contrary, many of the policies followed by a good many countries

Bank Act-Mr. Ilsley
ie.g., import and export restrictions, quotas, clearing agreements, etc). were such as to aggravate rather than to lessen the evils left by the war.
My second point is that in the twenties and the early thirties the Canadian banking system was subject to a clearly marked limitation which has since been remedied. I refer to the absence of a central bank.
During the period of rapid development of Canada as a nation, our banking system served this country extremely well. That is the universal verdict of foreign observers; it is, I think, the verdict of most Canadians. In this connection, I wish to quote a paragraph from the report of the royal commission on banking and currency in Canada, 1933. The paragraph reads as follows:
201. It has been manifest, from what we have previously written, and indeed from much of the information afforded us in the course of our hearings, that in so far as t'he ordinary functions of banking are concerned, the Canadian banks give admirable evidence of security, efficiency and convenience. In a time of universal economic difficulty, the Canadian banks have stood firm and have continued to render to the people of the dominion the same high quality and the same wide variety of services as in the past.
I wish to associate myself with that tribute to the Canadian banks. Ours has been a banking system of unusual strength; thanks to the protections surrounding the incorporation of banks, the provisions designed to safeguard the note issue, the prohibition of loans upon real estate, and the diversification of risk which is inherent in the branch banking system, the losses suffered by the creditors of Canadian banks, their note holders and depositors, have been extremely small. The importance of this factor of strength or safety should have been brought home to us in the early thirties by the contrast with conditions in the United States where thousands of banks failed, bringing untold loss and hardship to millions of bank depositors and aggravating greatly the severity of the depression. Another merit of our system has been its flexibility and the elasticity of the currency supply which it provided. These virtues were the result of the absence of rigid legal reserve provisions, the issue of notes on the basis for the most part of the general assets of. the bank, and the branch banking system' which facilitated1 the automatic flow of credit in accordance with the seasonal credit requirements of various industries and various sections of the country. Their importance was particularly great in a country such as Canada with its wide climatic variations, its emphasis on primary industries, and the very special problem of moving the western grain crop to market each fall and winter.
The only other merit of the Canadian banking system to which I wish to refer is the comprehensive network of banking facilities which it has provided for the convenience of the public. There may be certain areas to-day where we find public criticism of the closing of branches since the early thirties. This criticism in itself is confirmation of the extent to which our banking system at its peak bad brought banking services to nearly every hamlet throughout the country. Even to-day Canada is probably still better served with banking facilities than almost any other country. The branch system made it possible to give services to hundreds of communities which could not otherwise have supported a bank, and for many years it was the pride of our Canadian banks that they pioneered the new communities, going in ahead of the railway or indeed of any sizeable population.
These and other merits of our banking system deserve great praise. It will be noted, however, that they relate primarily to the working of individual banking institutions and to the strict or narrow function of commercial banking. In certain respects the system as a whole left something to be desired. Thus up to 1935 the volume of money and credit in circulation in Canada was regulated essentially merely by competition amongst the chartered banks in the granting of loans and the purchase of securities. The banks, however, were private, profit-making institutions and it was only natural that the automatic working of competitive, commercial forces should not always coincide perfectly with the broadest national interest. Fortunately our banks were usually staffed with able, prudent and far-sighted men, and normally their business judgment led them, to make decisions and adopt policies which were not only sound for their institutions but also in the national interest. There may be some confirmation for this statement in the reported fact that Canada leads seventeen countries in the number of years of prosperity per year of depression. In an elaborate analysis of business cycles in various countries, published by the National Bureau of Economic Research, New York, under the title "Business Annals", Professors Thorp and Mitchell found that for the period 1888-1924 Canada had had 1-86 years of prosperity for each year of depression, while the United States had enjoyed but 1-79 years and the average for the seventeen countries studied was but 1-14 years.
However, as our economy became more and more industrialized and more sensitive to the rhythm of business fluctuations in other countries, it became more and more obvious that we needed a more delicate adjustment of the volume of credit to' real public requirements.
Bank Act-Mr. Ilstey

a more effective mechanism for endeavouring to counteract by credit control the normal tendency of business forces to alternate between boom and depression. In the late stages of a boom, as for instance in the late twenties, it was difficult for any individual banker or indeed for the group of commercial bankers as a whole to break away from the prevailing business and public psychology and ruthlessly apply the brakes against further expansion. Similarly when a boom collapsed, it was not always possible for the private banker, interested necessarily in the safety of his institution and the protection of his depositors, to follow an expansionist credit-granting policy which might have tended to retard the process of deflation. One can scarcely Dlame a group of competing banks for failing to discharge with 100 per cent perfection a function for which they were not assigned specific responsibility by public authority. The fault lay rather in the failure of public policy to provide an institution charged with responsibility for regulating the volume of money and credit solely in the public interest. Such a function could only be performed by a public body interested not in the making of profits but solely in the performance of a public duty.
It was the lack of such an entity which the Macmillan commission found as the one important defect of the Canadian banking system, as a result of their investigations during the summer of 1933. As they expressed it, they were impressed "by the absence in Canada of any single banking authority which while linked by its activities with national finance and commerce, is nevertheless detached by its constitution and the temper of its administration from the ordinary pursuits of commercial banking." In other words, they found no organization charged with responsibility for regulating the volume of credit and currency in the best interests of the economic life of the nation. On the basis of this finding, they recommended the establishment of a central bank in Canada. The following year parliament passed the necessary legislation and on March 11, 1935, the Bank of Canada commenced operations.
This development marked the beginning of a series of reforms, designed to improve our banking system and secure a rounding out and better integration of our financial structure as a whole, a series of reforms which we expect to carry much farther during the present session of parliament. One of these reforms related to the organization of the Bank of Canada itself. The House will remember that as the bank was originally organized, its stock

was held by private shareholders, although the bank was subject to strict control by the government. An important amendment to the act in 1938 eliminated the private shareholders and made the bank a government-owned as well as a government-controlled institution. Since that amendment, there can be no question that the control of currency and credit in this country is carried out by a public institution solely in the public interest. Concurrently with these developments and assisted greatly by the Bank of Canada, there has come a very much improved organization of the short-term money market in Canada; the issue of treasury bills at public tender at very low rates of interest and the active markets for short-term securities generally are reflections of this development. In 1939 an attempt was made to improve the organization of, and the practices in, the longterm mortgage market, and an act authorizing the setting up of a central mortgage bank was passed by parliament. Unfortunately the war intervened just as this bank was on the point of being set up and action to implement this legislation had to be deferred. In all probability parliament will find it necessary in the not distant future to reenact this legislation in a modified form in order to standardize and make more marketable mortgage credit instruments and thereby make possible more economical long-term credit. The banking and commerce committee has now before it a bill to authorize the establishment of an industrial development bank, which is designed to fill another gap in our financial structure- the provision on reasonable terms of fixed and working capital for small or new industrial enterprises whose needs are not met,^ or not fully met, by existing financial institutions. Finally, the speech from the throne has indicated that we intend to introduce a bill to authorize the insurance or guarantee ^ of export credits in order to assist in developing export markets for primary and secondary industries in the post-war period.
When we add to the measures which I have listed the significant proposals which we are making in the Bank Act amending bill and in the supplementary legislation to which I shall refer in a moment, the house will agree, I trust, that a very serious effort has been and is being made to build up in this country^ a well-rounded and highly integrated financial structure which, with the changes still to come, should be able to take care of all the sound credit needs of the Canadian public. The bill which is now before the house represents the results of a thorough and painstaking study of our existing Bank Act and of the

Bank Act-Mr. Ilsley
changes which should be made in it to enable our chartered banks to meet present day needs. I do not flatter myself that it will meet the views or satisfy the wishes of all groups and individual members in this house. It will not, of course, satisfy those whose doctrines lead them to advocate the nationalization of the banks as a step towards the overthrow of private enterprise, nor those who cannot withstand the temptation of making free credit available in a way which in my view would result in the debasement of our monetary system. The changes I am proposing are intended to improve our banking system and to ensure adequate credit at [DOT] reasonable rates for all sound and useful purposes. We are suggesting those improvements which can be achieved by legislative means, but in my opinion we should be foolhardy indeed to reorganize it completely along radical lines as a matter of political doctrine or tactics, or to tamper with its integrity and exploit it in accordance with the theories of the inflationist school.
Let me deal first with the demand of one of the parties in this house that the banks should be nationalized. In preparing to meet this argument, I tried to find out just what was the case for nationalization, or rather, what its advocates felt the case to be. As usual, I found a great many vague charges against existing institutions, a great deal of loose and irresponsible indictment, far too much appeal to popular prejudice and a great many rosy promises in regard to what might be expected to happen under a new dispensation, but very little analysis of what was regarded as wrong under the present system and very little in the way of concrete proposals-

speechtext:
-indeed little more than a mere beckoning to the promised land with a minimum of specifications as to how to reach it and none as to how our lives would be ordered when we get there.
Trying to put the pieces together, I find that there are apparently four arguments or contentions used by its advocates to support the case for bank nationalization. They may be summarized as follows:
First, the argument that nationalization of banks is necessary in order to make possible the effective control of currency, credit and prices;
Secondly, the contention that nationalization of banks will result in greater economy and efficiency;
Thirdly, the claim that the banks are a monopoly or through the system of interlocking directorates constitute part of a "big business" monopoly; and
Finally, the argument that nationalization of the banks is necessary as the first step in bringing about the end of private enterprise and ushering in the socialist state.
Well, let us see, if we can, what there is in each of these contentions.
Take the first argument. It is, of course, essential that the state-that is the government, responsible to parliament and the people- should have control over the total volume of bank credit, in order that such credit may be regulated as a measure of economic policy in the general interest. But as I have taken pains to point out, we already have that control in the hands of the government, exercised through the Bank of Canada as its agent. This control over bank credit is effected by the Bank of Canada through its control over the cash reserves of the chartered banks. Because of the nature of their business and well-defined practices of long standing, it is necessary for the banks to limit their deposits to about ten times their cash reserves. That is to say, the banks find it necessary to keep about $1 in reserves in the form of Bank of Canada notes or deposits with the Bank of Canada for each $10 which they owe to their depositors. The law reenforced this established practice by prescribing that in no event shall a bank have cash reserves of less than 5 per cent of its deposit liabilities. In fact however, the practical necessity of the ten to one ratio has been so well established in practice that the legal obligation is of comparatively minor significance.
On the other hand, the need to earn interest in order to pay interest on its deposits, meet its other operating expenses and earn some profit on its capital, drives each bank to increase its loans or its investments to the point where its cash reserves come down to the ratio which prudence and well-established practice require. This spur of cost and self-interest therefore ensures that cash reserves do not significantly exceed ten per cent of a bank's deposits, and therefore that total deposits of all the banks closely approximate ten times the total amount of cash reserves which is held by all the banks. (It would of course be more accurate for me to speak of total demand liabilities or total note and deposit liabilities, but as bank notes are now such a small and decreasing portion of



Bank Act-Mr. Ilsley
their total liabilities, I am, for simplicity's sake, speaking as if bank deposits were the only form of bank credit.)
For the reasons mentioned, the Bank of Canada has effective control of the total volume of bank credit outstanding.' It exercises that control through its control over the cash reserves of the chartered banks. These reserves are made up of Bank of Canada notes and deposits with the Bank of Canada. They are watched closely and are expanded or contracted as the public interest may seem to require. The Bank of Canada can reduce them by selling some its large holdings of government securities. It gets paid for such securities by a cheque drawn on a chartered bank, which when presented for payment, results in a reduction in that bank's deposit with the Bank of Canada. Conversely, if the Bank of Canada wishes to expand bank reserves-in order to promote an expansion in bank deposits or bank credit-it can do so very easily by purchasing government securities on the open market. It pays for such securities by a cheque drawn upon itself which is deposited in a chartered bank by the person or business firm selling the security, and when the chartered bank presents the cheque to the Bank of Canada it gets an increase in its deposits with the Bank of Canada-or takes out Bank of Canada notes to hold in its reserves.
This process of control of bank reserves, find thereby of bank deposits and bank credit, is well known to many members of this house, but I felt it should be reviewed here to make clear beyond any doubt that already the government has effective control over the total volume of money and credit. We have the control we need for all the essential purposes of monetary policy. Moreover, we have it in an exceedingly simple form which enables us to exercise over-all control without interference in the granting of individual credits or the transfer of deposits or any of the other business transactions of an individual bank. Any one bank is free to compete for all the business it can get-because it can attract deposits and thereby cash reserves away from the other banks. It is free to exercise sound business judgment in the selection of its risks and the choice of its customers. Hence the credit control we exercise is a sensible form of national economic planning and direction in matters of broad policy, free from the dead hand of bureaucratic interference in private affairs. I only wish such simple and effective mechanisms of national control and stimulus were available in other equally important fields of economic activity.

It should now be clear that the need for public direction of monetary policy does not necessitate nor justify the socialization of all our banks. It requires only socialization of central banking-and that of course we have already achieved.
Now if there is no justification for nationalization in the first argument used by its advocates, is there any in the second, the possibility of greater efficiency and economy as a result of state operated banks? There are few, I think, who would seriously charge that our chartered banks are inefficient. The various departments and agencies under my direction have had a great deal of experience in dealing with the chartered banks-the Department of Finance with its enormous disbursements and receipts; the national war finance committee in the sale and handling of victory bonds; the foreign exchange control board in the carrying out of our external transactions, public and private; the wartime prices and trade board in the complicated business of ration coupon banking; as well as the Bank of Canada in its operations as a central bank, and the inspector general of banks in his intimate audit of all the banks. All this experience with chartered banks and knowledge of their detailed working confirms the general belief in the efficiency of the chartered banks in carrying out the normal functions of commercial banking. Certainly I think there would be few who would honestly contend that the banks would be operated more efficiently or more economically as one great department or agency of government. Like other large organizations they must have their own problems of bureaucracy, must face the same difficulties as we do in reconciling central control with local initiative. It is absurd to assert that these problems and these difficulties would be solved and greater efficiency and economy promoted by a far greater centralization under direct public or political control and with neither the lash of competition nor the spur of profit possibilities.
The third argument of the nationalization advocates rests on the charge of monopoly, the allegation that the banks themselves are a monopoly or form part of a larger group which' in some way or other constitutes a monopoly and exercises control over the industrial and financial institutions of Canada. I am sure that we shall hear the changes rung on this contention and that long lists of the company connections of various bank directors will be presented. The argument has a certain specious appeal. It is easy to make. It can be made in vague terms and embellished

Bank Act

Mr. Ilsley
with innuendo. It can be used to stir prejudice against mere bigness and successful achievement. But the only point which should interest a responsible member of this house is whether or not it is true.
No one, of course, will wish to deny that most bank directors are also on the boards of other financial or industrial corporations, in a number of cases on a good many other boards. I suppose the quality which above all others the banks desire in their directors is sound business judgment and it seems only natural therefore that they should seek their directors amongst men who have proven they possess that quality by the success they have achieved in other businesses. If the community's banking needs are to be efficiently served, we need men of large vision, constructive imagination, sound judgment and wide experience to assist in formulating the general policies which are to be applied by the senior executive officers of the banks. It would, I think, be very unfortunate if the day ever comes in this country when demonstrated success in one line of business, proven capacity for the direction of large affairs, should debar a man from bringing the benefit of his judgment, foresight and experience to the assistance of bank managements or the management of any other business or, I may add, to the direction of public affairs. Canada has great natural resources and will have adequate capital, but the speed of her future growth and development will depend as much as anything on the adequacy of her supply of managerial talent, of business leaders who possess the qualities which I have mentioned. As a nation we should encourage that kind of talent, not discourage it or decry its success.
Let no one mistake my position. I am not arguing for a widespread use of interlocking directorates but merely for a rational approach to this problem. I have no brief for the man who spreads himself thin over a long list of directorates, and I often wish that the banks and other business corporations would search more intently for suitable directorship material in other walks of life-such as in small business, agriculture and labour-and also that the banks would use to a greater extent the device of regional advisory committees in order to obtain the benefit of as many points of view as possible in working out their policies. These suggestions are merely personal, but I think their adoption would do a great deal to bring about a better public understanding of bank operations and policies and should remove even the appearance of any grounds for the charge that banks are run by a monopoly of big business men in the interest of big business. I suspect that bankers themselves will feel their own consciences clear in this respect
100-160i
and may not see the need of any such devices as I have suggested. They will resent, and rightly so, the insinuation that because they have directors from this and that corporation on their board they allow themselves to be dominated by them, particularly to the extent of restricting credit to the competitors of those corporations. That is a very serious imputation and I do not for a moment believe it has any foundation. No director is allowed to be present or vote at a particular meeting when loans or advances to himself or any firm or corporation in which he is a partner or a director are under consideration, and I am convinced that any director who attempted to prevent the bank from meeting the credit needs of a competitor would receive short shrift at the hands of his fellow directors. If there is any honourable member who honestly believes otherwise, he will have his chance in court. Let him cross-question the bankers when they come before the banking and commerce committee and he will find out how the banks really operate.
After all; there are two tests of whether the banks constitute a monopoly. The first is whether in fact the banks fail to compete with each other in the obtaining of deposit accounts and the granting of credits and thus tend to promote a restriction of credit. The second is whether the banks make abnormal or monopoly profits. Taking the second question first, I am going to give in a few moments detailed figures of the earnings of Canadian banks over a long period. If, after I have disclosed this previously unpublished information, there is any one who still believes that the banks are obtaining abnormal or monopoly profits it will be, I am afraid, because "one convinced against his will is of the same opinion still". On the first point we have the testimony of the volume, "Social Planning for Canada," which according to the foreword written by the late Mr. Woodsworth is "the first comprehensive treatise on Canadian economy from a socialist point of view." I quote the following extract from its discussion of Canadian banks:
Before answering this question, it is as well to make clear how the chartered, banks operate to-day. Their operations are regulated, of course, 'by a bank act enacted by the federal government, from whom they derive their charters. Perhaps because of this regulation the Canadian banks have been free from the sort of defect which plunged the whole American banking system into panic in 1933. Canadian banks have kept clear of the worst type of speculative loan (e.g., real estate). No bank failure has taken place in Canada since the Home bank closed in 1924. Nothing comparable to the disclosures made with respect to the investment activities of the big banks in the United States has emerged in Canada. At the
Bank Act-Mr. Ilsley

same time the competition between the banks would seem to guarantee reasonably fair and competitive treatment of all comers.
In general then-and certainly from any superficial point of view-the chartered banks .present a picture of a stable, well-ordered set of institutions; a tower of strength in time of trouble, as they not infrequently remind us. There is no doubt that a defective banking system enormously aggravates the inherent instability of the capitalist system; and Canada has been spared that complication.
Most of the current criticism of the chartered banks is picayune stuff. . . .
There can be no doubt about the competition for deposit accounts; even though the banks pay the same rate of interest on deposits there are other ways in which the keen competition manifests itself, including the character and variety of the services offered. Equally there can be no doubt of the competition for lending accounts and an even greater possibility of variation between the different banks in the treatment given and in the services rendered. Business men, both large and small, accustomed to dealing with banks will bear witness to competition that takes place between the banks in attracting accounts. If one talks to such business men one will not take long in finding many instances of switches of lending accounts from one bank to another. Obviously, banks turn down certain applications for loans but the reason is almost certain to be, at least in times other than those of acute depression, either that it was not the type of a loan that a bank should make or that the particular borrower or business was unlikely to be able to repay the loan. In the latter type of case there is always -recourse for the borrower to one or all of the other nine banks who may take a different view of the credit-worthiness of the borrower or his enterprise. It is -most unreasonable to think that the banks, at least in normal times, should deliberately wish to refuse sound loans or -restrict credits when they have the resources with which to make loans. If they cannot get commercial loans, their only recourse is to invest their funds in securities. On such securities they earn less, usually much less, than they could make on sound commercial loans. To-day, and for some years past, their percentage of loans to total assets has been unduly low. The desire to increase their earnings, if nothing else, drives them to seek outlets in loans. The charge of a monopolistic combination conspiring to restrict credit is a figment of the imagination and has no foundation whatever.
The fourth and final point with which we have to deal is the argument that nationalization of the banks is the first step necessary in the liquidation of private enterprise and

the ushering in of the socialist state. I suspect that here we have the crux of the whole case. To those who are convinced socialists, it must seem reasonably obvious that control of the banks and other financial institutions is probably an indispensable instrument for the liquidation or slow strangulation of free enterprise and for ushering in the new dispensation. Certainly it will immensely facilitate the task and it is equally clear that a privately controlled banking system would not be consistent with a socialized state.
If we were all socialists, this argument would be wholly convincing. The simple and conclusive answer to it is that the Canadian people are not socialists and do not want to adopt devices, the only valid argument for which is that they will facilitate the coming of socialism. No one can tell me that the Canadian people who have reacted as they have in the last three or four years to the limited controls and partial regimentations essential to the emergency requirements of wartime would ever vote to imprison themselves in a socialist state which would make such controls and regimentations practically universal and perpetual.
If we do not want a socialist state, we do not want a socialized commercial banking system to deaden the initiative of our system of free enterprise. We do not want this government or any other government to have a monopoly of the business of lending for commercial purposes nor even of the business of keeping the people's banking accounts. The relation between banker and borrower, and between banker and depositor is a private, confidential relationship. A large proportion of our citizens would not want any government, even one which they support, to intervene in this confidential relationship or to be privy to it. But a far more important point is the undesirability of having the credit of each of us and of every business throughout the country assessed by civil servants working under political control for a government banking monopoly, rather than by bank managers interested not in the political or other views of the borrower but solely in his ability and trustworthiness as a debtor. The best guarantee of fair lending as well as sound lending is to preserve a number of independent lending agencies, so that a potential borrower can choose his own banker, can deal with the one who is prepared to meet his credit requirements on the most favourable terms and who is interested solely in the soundness of the loan itself. We must, and we do, have control of the cash reserves of the banks, so that the total volume of all bank credit can be con-

Bank Act-Mr. Ilsley
trolled-and conditions of depression and crisis avoided. Given that, I think we can trust the enterprise of the banks to lend where opportunities for sound loans are available, because of the incentive to get their loanable funds earning a more attractive return than is possible under the only alternative of investing in securities.
There will be some cases where it would be illegal or inappropriate for the banks to make loans although the loan might be essentially sound and useful in developing Canadian industry and resources. We are proposing to meet this type of problem in two ways. First, we are proposing to establish the industrial development bank in order to assist the financing of small or new enterprises which might otherwise find it impossible or very difficult to get the types of credit required from banks or other financial institutions on reasonable terms and conditions. Here we are using the device of public ownership to carry out a specific task for which it is best fitted. But this government bank will have no monopoly; any potential borrower will be free to go first, or instead, to other banks or to any other source of capital if he so desires. Secondly, I shall be making proposals in a later section of my remarks which will involve assistance from the government to encourage loans to farmers and fishermen of a longer term and different character from those they have been able formerly to make. These two measures, I believe, will be sufficient when coupled with the other legislation announced in the speech from the throne to ensure that adequate credit will be made available for the efficient and vigorous development of our country. They are not intended either to drive the banks out of business or to be a means of gaining financial control over all kinds of business as a step towards socialism.
They do not throw into the scrap basket all *the heritage of the past. They build upon it and supplement it in order to remedy any defects it may have had and to enable it to meet fully and efficiently the requirements of our people. Like the nationalization of the Bank of Canada in 1938, they demonstrate the government's willingness to use the agency of the state, even the device of public ownership as well as control, where it is required to serve a useful and specific purpose. The question of nationalization of an industry or a specific firm should not be one of ideology. We should neither shrink from nationalization because of an economic philosophy based on fear, nor embrace it rashly with nothing more in our minds and hearts than mere devotion to doctrine or desire to punish. We should use it only where it alone can serve the public
interest or can serve it better than any alternative form of organization. Commercial banking, I am convinced, is not one of those cases. I hold that conviction with greater assurance, because I find that in no other democratic country have the people become convinced that it would be wise to nationalize their commercial banks. In thia connection it seems pertinent to observe that even the labour, and avowedly socialist, governments of Australia and New Zealand have not yet seen fit to nationalize the commercial banks in those two dominions.
Summing up this discussion, we find that the several alleged arguments for nationalization of the banks do not stand careful scrutiny. It is not necessary to nationalize the commercial banks to make possible the effective control of currency, credit and prices; we have already nationalized that part of the monetary and banking system which gives us control over currency, credit and prices, namely the central bank. There is no reason, on grounds of operating efficiency, for nationalization. There is no basis for the charge that the chartered banks, whether in combination with other business or not, constitute a monopoly which interferes with the free flow of credit and leads to monopoly profits. We do not want nationalization to promote the liquidation or strangulation of free enterprise or as the entering wedge for socialism. We are providing a publicly-owned institution to provide credit for useful and desirable industrial projects which the private institutions are unable or unwilling to finance, but we do not want to create a huge government monopoly of the banking business which would lead to an enormous increase in centralization, a loss in operating efficiency, a decline in the initiative and enterprise which decentralized and competing private business is best able to supply, and the inevitable intrusion of political consideration and control in the multitude of private transactions which the banks must make. We are confirmed in our point of view by the experience of all other democratic countries.
I would now like to spend a few minutes on what I understand to be the position of the Social Credit party. Their attack on the banking system will be of an entirely different character from that of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party. They, or at least most of them, recognize, I believe, that the chartered banks are efficient in carrying out the ordinary day-to-day functions of commercial banking and would, I imagine, dislike as much as I do the socialist proposal to convert the banks into a huge government monopoly run by bureaucrats. I do not think I need to devote any attention to the main, or
Bank Act-Mr. Ilsley

shall I say, the original, body of their doctrine, which has been discussed in this house on several occasions and which we seem to hear much less of to-day.
To judge from their more recent utterances, what we may expect from the Social Credit party in this debate is likely to be a proposal that the government should borrow its requirements from the Bank of Canada and that the resulting increase in Bank of Canada notes and deposits will be turned over almost entirely by their recipients to the chartered banks-since the public do not hold deposits in the Bank of Canada and hold only wyhat notes are needed for convenience-should be "frozen" in the hands of the chartered banks. In other words, the chartered banks should not be allowed to use these additional cash reserves as a basis for the usual tenfold expansion of their deposits. Presumably, they will suggest that this policy be carried out by amending the Bank Act in such a way as to require the banks to hold 100 per cent reserves against increases in their deposits beyond a specified figure. The purpose of such a restriction upon the activities of the banks would be to enable the government to borrow its requirements without paying interest except to itself by way of its agency, the Bank of Canada, and without allowing this increase in Bank of Canada money to lead to an unnecessary and very great addition to the loans, investments and deposits of the chartered banks, an addition that they recognize would probably lead to inflation.
Let us trace for a moment in simple terms just how this type of 100 per cent reserve arrangement would work, as undoubtedly many people are attracted by the easy virtues of this apparently costless source of credit. Suppose, then, that we did rule that the banks could not use any additional cash reserve which they obtain, in consequence of government borrowing from the Bank of Canada, as the basis for the usual tenfold expansion in deposits-or what would amount to the same thing, that they must hold additional cash reserves equal to any additions to their present level of deposits. Let us concentrate on the main, simple point and neglect the purely technical difficulties. Armed with this shield against the expansion of bank credit, the government will proceed, we may assume, to borrow, say $1 billion, from the Bank of Canada. With this new fund the government would then draw cheques on the Bank of Canada payable to contractors, civil servants, holders of government bonds and others to whom it must make payments for services rendered. The recipients of these cheques deposit them in

their bank account in the normal way, as they do any other cheque-taking in cash from their banks only what they need to have to carry around in the form of cash. The chartered banks will then find that their deposits have increased by almost the whole amount of this billion dollars and in exchange they will have these cheques on the Bank of Canada less the small amount paid out in cash to depositors-which we may safely neglect merely to simplify the argument. The chartered banks then present the cheques to the Bank of Canada and their deposits with that bank increase by $1 billion.
At this stage then the chartered banks' deposit liabilities have increased by about a billion dollars and their cash reserves-their assets-have increased by a billion dollars While their books may balance they are very much worse off than before because they must pay interest on the additional deposits, so far as these are in the form of savings deposits, and provide services on them which cost real money, and no small amount of money at that as I shall seek to show later. On the other hand, the increase in their assets which is in the form of cash reserves brings in no income at all, as the Bank of Canada, of course, pays no interest on its deposits.
It is in this unfavourable position that the banks would be frozen by the amendment which I suggested the Social Crediters might propose. The banks would be prevented absolutely from following the normal course of using part of their additional reserves to make additional loans or buy additional securities, which is the means by which bank credit and thus bank deposits are expanded on the basis of the additional reserves. It is the expansion made possible in loans and investments under the usual practice that enables the banks to cover the costs of the additions to their deposit liabilities. To block this normal expansion in order to make it safe for the government to exploit Bank of Canada credit more fully, means depriving the banks of the means of meeting the additional cost. As a result, either the shareholders of the bank must absorb these increased costs by receiving less earnings or * suffering losses, or the depositors must pay the costs through higher service charges or reduced interest on savings deposits, or other borrowers from the banks must pay more, or bank employees must get less in the form of wages and salaries, or all or some of the four groups must share the burden between them.
It should now be possible to see the proposal in its true light. It is a proposal that the

Bank Act-Mr. Ilsley
government through the Bank of Canada should force the chartered banks to borrow from the public in the form of deposits which are of course liabilities or debts of the banks, at a cost either in interest or in services rendered, and to relend the funds so obtained to the government interest free. Obviously, such a system favours the government as a borrower. It enables the government to obtain not debt-free money as is contended by its advocates because notes and deposits are liabilities of the body which issues them, but rather interest-free loans. Obviously, also, the system is merely a complicated device for obtaining forced ' loans from the banks and either the shareholders, the depositors, or the borrowing clients or the employees of the banks must suffer the losses which are the government's gain. This is nothing less than taxation of a most discriminatory and unfair character. There is no reason why the government should seek to escape the cost of interest on its borrowings at the expense of any one or all of these particular groups associated with the banks. The only equitable policy is for the government to pay reasonable rates of interest appropriate to the form and nature of the borrowing and meet the cost from taxation levied by parliament in the way considered fairest and most equitable. If we must for any reason raise forced loans, they should be raised as a general measure applicable fairly to all in accordance with their ability to pay.
Now, I do not think such proposals would be seriously put forward by members of this house, if it were not for the belief which seems to be prevalent in certain quarters that banking is a costless function. We have heard so much talk in recent years about the ten to one ratio and so much propaganda about "fountain-pen money" that some people have come to believe that it costs banks little or nothing to carry on their operations, that it is a very simple business concerned almost entirely with holding a fountain pen upside down and letting the ink run, and that of course the banks must be making enormous profits. The facts are quite to the contrary and something at least of their general signi-finance should, I would have thought, be familiar to certain hon. members who belong to the Social Credit party. They at least should be familiar with the Public Accounts of the province of Alberta which show, if I read them correctly, that the Alberta treasury branches which operate certain deposit accounts had an excess of expenditures over
revenue of roughly $390,000 on their operations during the fiscal year 1942-43, and even if we exclude the consumers bonus which was paid, a loss of S246,000.
I am quoting these figures to show that banking is not a costless function.

Total operating expenditures, after deducting this bonus and, by the way, without including any rentals of office space, were $368,000. As total deposits at the end of that year amounted to less than $6,900,000, this would appear to indicate that the cost to the Alberta government of operating these accounts was something over 5-3 per cent. This seems to throw some light on the cost of operating a deposit business.
While the facts as to bank operating costs and earnings refute some of the views currently held, I am convinced that they must be seen in order to be believed. I have therefore come to the considered conclusion that I should break a long-established tradition of Canadian banking and disclose to this house the essential facts in regard to the operations of the Canadian banking system as a whole.
If therefore the house will permit me, I will place on Hansard, at this point a statement showing the current operating earnings and the current operating expenses of the Canadian banks as a group for the average of the fifteen years 1929-43 as well as for the year 1943, together with certain supplementary information relating to the amount of dividends paid to shareholders, the net amount of current operating earnings available for losses on loans, investments and other assets and for general contingencies, the net amount of capital profits including certain nonrecurring profits, and the average annual amount required during the 15-year period for losses or specific provision for losses on loans, investments and other assets, less recoveries.

speechtext:
Bank Act-Mr. llsley
I will call attention to a few of the more significant points disclosed by this table. The average annual current operating earnings for the 15-year period were $138-7 millions or 4-02 per cent on total assets. These total figures are broken down into interest and discount on loans, earnings on securities and exchange, commission, service charges and other operating earnings, but I will not weary the house by quoting the detailed figures. Current operating expenses (not including losses) averaged $112-3 for the 15-year period which was 3-26 per cent on total assets. These expenses are classified under six headings. When we compare this figure of current operating earnings of only 4-02 per cent of total assets with operating expenses of 3-26 per cent, we have to conclude that there must be something wrong with this fountain pen theory and that the operating margin on which banks have to work is a fairly thin one.
The supplementary information shows that dividends paid to shareholders averaged only 4-6 per cent of total shareholders' equity over the last fifteen years. Even if we take total shareholders' net income which is the sum of dividends, net capital profits, including nonrecurring profits, and net current earnings available for losses less the average annual net amount required for losses, we find that it amounted to only 5-09 per cent of total shareholders' equity on the average for the 15-year period. By no stretch of the imagination can a business which produces such results be regarded as a gold mine.
There is just one further point I would wish to make. The table which I have presented shows that after paying dividends which cannot be regarded as high, there was available, out of current operating earnings, for losses on loans, investments and other assets and for general contingencies only an average annual amount of $12-8 million. To this figure are to be added certain net capital profits, averaging $2-5 million a year. This figure includes certain non-recurring profits, among them the profit on gold in the year 1935 and certain profits on securities. In this latter connection. it must be remembered that the 15-year period was one in which there was a substantial reduction in interest rates, leading to a corresponding increase in bond prices. Against the sums available out of current operating earnings and from capital profits must be set the requirements for losses or specific provision for losses on loans, investments and other assets, losses which must be expected in the business of banking over a period of years. For the 15-year period, those requirements after deducting any recoveries in 100-161
respect of losses over-provided for in earlier years average $13-8 million per year. This is the average or "normal" loss experience during this period of good and bad years; everyone knows that the losses in the early thirties were much higher, requiring in certain cases the transfer of substantial sums from published reserves to inner reserves. It is clear from the table that our banking system has fortunately been able to absorb those losses and in addition that it must have strengthened its inner reserve over the last fifteen years by an average annual amount of modest size. Is there any hon. member who will take the responsibility of expressing the conviction that that amount is unduly large for a banking system which is the trustee of the people's savings and which has increased its assets and, therefore, its liabilities by no less than 62 per cent during the period in question.
It js true that interest being paid on savings deposits is now lower than it was on the average during the 15-year period and the total assets and the volume of business of the banks have increased under wartime conditions. On the other hand, the average rate of return on securities and other earning assets of the banks has decreased. The table shows that for the year 1943, total current operating earnings of the banks amounted to $144-5 million or only 2-86 per cent on the total assets of the banks. Current operating expenses, on the other hand, were $114-9 million or 2-28 per cent on total assets. The margin between operating earnings and operating expenses of the banks therefore was somewhat lower than the average for the 15-year period. I am speaking now about the year 1943. Dividends paid to shareholders in 1943 were only 3-3 per cent of total shareholders' equity, and even total shareholders' net income last year was only 6-03 per cent of shareholders' equity. Even in a good year like 1943 the total amount left over out of current operating earnings and capital profits available foT losses or specific provision for losses and for general contingencies was only $22-0 million, although there had been a reduction in dividends paid by nearly all the banks, thus retaining for this purpose funds which would normally have been paid out. I have already pointed out that the average annual requirement for losses or specific provision for losses during the last fifteen years was $13-8 million. Under the circumstances and bearing in mind that the losses of bad years have to be met out of the earnings of good years such as 1943, it will be obvious that last year's net earnings were not unduly large.

Bank Act-Mr. Ilsley

As Minister of Finance it is my responsibility to exercise general, supervision over the operations of the Canadian banks and that is a responsibility which I take very seriously. My considered judgment is that the Canadian banks. have not made unduly large profits, that they have come through a most difficult period without impairing the proud tradition of safety which they have built up over a long period of years, that they have reserved an amount of earnings appropriate to take care of the normal hazards of banking but not an amount which responsible and prudent men could say is unduly large, and that their shareholders have been content with a net amount of earnings, both in the form of dividends and left in the business, which is really modest by comparison with the record of other businesses subject to similar risks and managed with comparable efficiency.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONDITIONS GOVERNING TEN-YEAR EXTENSION OP BANK CHARTERS
speechtext:
Major changes in the Bank Act. Apart from the extension of the charters of the ten existing banks for a further ten-year period ending July 1, 1954, the bill which is now before the house contains a great many amendments to our existing legislation as a result of the very thorough examination we
[Mr. Ilsley.1
have made of that legislation. Many of these are consequential in character or of minor importance and I shall call the attention of the house only to those of major importance.
First let me deal with the new provisions relating to the issue of notes by the chartered banks. Hon. members will recall that under the existing act the banks have been required to reduce their note issue gradually during the last ten years. As a result of this requirement the legal limit of their note issue in Canada on January 1, 1945, was to be 25 per cent of the amount of their unimpaired, paid-up capital, and what was to happen thereafter was to depend on a further enactment by parliament. During the present year the legal limit is 35 per cent, but the house will realize that in practice the banks must operate somewhat below this legal limit.
We have given very careful consideration to whether-we should prohibit further note issue altogether or provide for a further gradual reduction in the legal limit of issue or provide for a continuance of the 25 per cent legal limit which without further enactment would be the law as from January 1 next. We were impressed by the fact that since the establishment of the Bank of Canada, note issue of the chartered banks has ceased to play the important role it formerly played in our economy, and impressed also with the desirability of having all our " money," in the narrow sense of the term (that is to say, coins and paper money) issued by an agency of the state rather than by private institutions. Moreover, from the {mint 0f view of the banks I think it can no longer be said that the small amount of notes which they are now permitted to issue can be of any great value in promoting efficiency and economy in the operations of the banks. We have therefore recast the relevant sections of the act to accomplish the following purposes:
1.	to preclude any new bank that may be
incorporated from having any right to issue notes;
2.	to limit the right of existing banks to
issue and reissue notes in Canada to the period ending January 1, 1945, and in that period only up to the present limit of 35 per cent of their unimpaired, paid-up capital;
3.	to require the existing banks to reduce
their note issue in Canada by January 1, 1945, to 25 per cent of their unimpaired, paid-up capital; thereafter until January 1, 1950, to take away from them the right to issue o reissue their notes; and to require them to retire all their notes outstanding in Canada by January 1, 1950; and

Bank Act-Mr. llsley
4.	to allow existing banks to continue to issue notes for circulation outside of Canada but only up to a maximum of 10 per cent of their unimpaired, paid-up capital.
