On January 1, 1950, the amount of unretired notes issued for circulation to Canada and still outstanding must be paid over to the Bank of Canada and the Bank of Canada will then become liable to redeem the said notes. On the passing of the act the Bank of Canada will become the agency for redemption of the notes of any bank that winds up. Notes of those banks which have been wound up in the past will henceforth be redeemed by the Bank of Canada rather than by the Minister of Finance. It will be obvious that as a result of these proposals the Bank of Canada is to become after January 1, 1950, the exclusive note-issuing agency in Canada, and it will also be the exclusive note-redemption agency, first, of the outstanding notes of defunct banks, and by 1950, of any outstanding notes of the existing banks.
I should add that the changes which we are proposing in regard to note issue will require certain other consequential changes. Apart from the necessary changes in the statements regarding note issue required to be 100-161i
made to the minister, there will also be a new subsection providing that the provisions of the Act relating to the circulation redemption fund shall cease to operate in respect of any bank after it has paid over to the Bank of Canada the funds needed to redeem any of its notes outstanding on January 1, 1950.
I might at this point refer to a somewhat related amendment to section 92 of the act. The general principle as to the responsibility of a bank in respect of deposits made with it which has long been in effect in Canada, has been that the claim of a depositor is not barred or lost by reason of any statute of limitations or prescription, the responsibility of the bank being a continuing responsibility. I believe that this principle is just, and fundamental to maintaining confidence in the banking structure. A modification of the application of this principle is proposed by the amendment. If. in respect of any debt owing by a bank and outstanding on its books in Canada by reason of a deposit, no transaction has taken place and no claim has been made for ten years, or if in respect of any such debt owing by the bank by reason of a cheque, draft or bill of exchange issued, drawn or certified by it, no payment has been made for ten years, the bank shall pay to the Bank of Canada the amount of the debt together with interest, if any. to the date of payment. Thereupon the liability of the bank in respect of the debt ceases and determines but it is provided that the Bank of Canada shall, if payment is demanded by the person who was creditor of the bank or by his legal representatives, pay the amount paid to it together with interest, if interest was payable on the debt, for a period not exceeding twenty years at such rate and computed in such manner as may be determined from time to time by the governor in council. After the expiration of the twenty-year period the Bank of Canada will continue to be liable to pay the amount and the interest accumulated during that period, but no further interest will accumulate. The governor in council may make regulations prescribing the time for payment by a bank to the Bank of Canada, the records to be maintained or kept by the bank with reference to a debt with respect to which payment is so made, the manner of payment of any claim against the Bank of Canada and the rate of interest to be paid by the Bank of Canada and the manner of computation thereof. The result of this amendment is that the principle I have referred to, that the claim of a depositor or his legal representative, to repayment of moneys deposited in a bank is not limited in time, is preserved, but unclaimed deposits, which
Bank Act-Mr. Ilsley

formerly were retained indefinitely by the chartered banks will no longer be retained by them.
Provision is also made that a bank shall not be liable in respect of any act or omission relating to an account kept by the bank, which occurred or which is alleged to have occurred thirty years prior to the making of a claim in respect thereof. At the present time a bank maintains complete records of all its accounts whether they are still open or have closed for many years, because there is no time limit on the liability of the bank to give an accounting in respect of any of these accounts. The amendment is designed to relieve the banks of liability where items in its accounts have not been questioned for thirty years and will permit the banks to destroy records more than thirty years old, the maintenance and accommodation of which are presenting an ever expanding problem, particularly under today's conditions. This provision does not apply to accounts kept by the bank in respect of unclaimed deposits, the provision for which I have already mentioned.
Various changes are being made in the provisions of the act regarding the many statements and returns required to be made to the minister. Former sections 112-114 have been recast and renumbered as sections 112119 for purposes of clarification and to eliminate repetition. This has permitted the penalty sections relating to returns (former sections 154-162) to be consolidated into one section (section 158). Minor changes have also been made in the form of some of the returns in consequence of other changes made in the act or for other reasons and there have been certain deletions to avoid unnecessary duplication or because the relevant information no longer serves any useful purpose.
Very important changes are being made in respect of section 91. Subsection 1 of this section fixes the maximum rate of interest or discount which may be charged by any chartered bank. In keeping with the decline in interest rates which has occurred in recent years, this maximum rate is now being reduced from 7 per cent to 6 percent per annum. However, we are adding a new subsection which makes a far more radical change in Canadian banking practice and which will, I hope, make a really important contribution to public need. It has always seemed to me highly anomalous that while this parliament has passed an act authorizing small loan companies and personal money lendlers to make small .personal instalment loans on the basis of a charge for interest, and other costs of 2 per cent per month for loans extending
fMr. Ilsley.]
up to fifteeen months, nevertheless we have at the same time prevented our normal lending institutions, the chartered banks, from participating effectively or on any considerable scale in this type of business. The loans are for small amounts, the average, I believe, being around $150, they require to be repaid in small monthly or other periodic instalments, and collateral security is inadequate or lacking altogether. The result is that the costs of doing the business are high and the effective rate of interest must be proportionate or the loans will not be made. The only reason, I believe, why this house was convinced that the small loan companies should be allowed to charge a rate as high at 2 per cent per month was the belief that otherwise the necessitous borrowers who need these loans would be driven to pay higher, and indeed much higher, rates to so-called loan sharks. No one liked to approve a charge of 2 per cent a month and yet the alternative was far worse.
After very careful consideration, I became convinced that we should make it possible for the chartered banks to participate on a substantial scale in this type of business. They already have offices in easy access to the public throughout the country and should therefore be able to conduct the business on a more economical basis. I am therefore proposing that where a loan, evidenced by a promissory note, repayable in substantially equal instalments does not exceed $500 and is not secured otherwise than by endorsement of the note or by insurance on the life of the borrower in favour of the bank as the insured, the bank may charge discount or interest at a rate which, having regard to the term of the loan and the frequency of the instalments, does not exceed a rate of interest equivalent to the rate resulting from a discount of 5 per cent on a one-year loan repayable in equal monthly instalments. A 5 per cent discount on such a loan is equivalent to an effective interest rate of 9f per cent per annum, which, it will be noted, is considerably less than half the rate allowed to the small loan companies and personal money lenders. No other charge can be made by the bank in respect of such loans except, of course, interest at no higher rate on overdue' payments and the actual cost to the bank of insurance on the life of the borrower. This insurance will be term insurance taken out in the form of a blanket policy on the lives of all such borrowers and the cost is very low indeed-I believe about twenty-five cents per $100. I wish to emphasize that the loans covered by the special provisions of this

Bank Act-Mr. Ilsley
subsection will be unsecured loans and that loans to a borrower who is able to give ordinary collateral security will come under the maximum interest ceiling provided for in subsection 1.
For these new proposals I would like the benefit of very special consideration by the banking and commerce committee and this house. In my desire to keep maximum charges low I may easily have gone too far and I would like the committee to hear evidence from the banks as to whether it is really possible to do this type of business under the terms which I am here suggesting. Furthermore, while in the interest of simplicity and for the purpose of avoiding an odd or fractional rate of interest, I have expressed the ceiling in terms of a 5 per cent discount, it may be that the committee may prefer to express the ceiling in terms of a maximum rate of interest per month or per year. I shall be prepared to welcome the guidance of the committee in this respect also.
An amendment to section 85 is being suggested to facilitate the financing of alterations of, repairs to or installations on ships or vessels. Under the present law a bank may loan money to aid in the building of a ship, taking as security therefor a mortgage, hypothec or lien on the ship. Under the amendment proposed they may take the same security for a loan to assist in the installation of engines or equipment or the repair or alteration of the ship or its engines or equipment.
There is also an amendment to section 75 which gives specific power to the banks to lend money or make advances upon the security of, and take as collateral security for any loan or advance made by it, lien or other notes, conditional sales contracts or any other instruments or agreements made or entered into respecting the sale of goods, wares and merchandise. The object of this amendment is to remove any doubt as to the validity of advances made on this type of security. Practically all notes taken for goods sold on a time basis are either in lien form or supported by lien contracts, and frequently the dealer who sells the goods or the finance company with whom he discounts the notes, desires to obtain bank credit against the security of such notes.
I now come to a series of amendments relating to a category of loans which, in banking parlance, is known as section 88 loans. There are a number of changes in the definitions in section 2 which have the effect of extending the coverage of section 88 and
making it possible for certain additional borrowers to get credit thereby. Thus the definition of "grain" is now widened to include "beans, and all kinds of seeds" and the definition of "live stock" is being extended to include fur-bearing animals in order to assist farmers and others who raise such animals for their pelts or for sale as breeders. Similarly, the definition of "manufacturer" has been extended to include bottlers and canners of all kinds. There are certain other important changes in regard to farmers and fishermen which I shall come to a little later.
In addition to these changes, I am also submitting for consideration certain proposed amendments to sections 88-90 and the schedules relevant thereto. Some of these amendments are intended to eliminate repetitions and certain inconsistencies but others are designed to simplify the procedure in giving security which is now complicated and believed to be unnecessarily burdensome on both borrowers and banks. AVe have received representations not only from banks but also from business firms and organizations requesting this simplification. After careful consideration, the arguments appeared to me to be convincing and I have therefore included the proposed amendments in the bill. However, I would like the banking and commerce committee to give these proposed amendments very carefully consideration and to hear evidence from both business and bankers in regard to them.
Perhaps I can make clearer the nature of the proposed amendments if I say a few words about the working of the present section and the arguments which have been advanced for the suggested changes. Manufacturers constantly process raw materials into finished goods which are sold and new materials are continually being purchased for manufacture. Other types of borrowers likewise find it necessary frequently to turn over the goods upon which security is given. Under the terms of section 88, as it is at present, fresh security must be given every time new materials are acquired. This involves a good deal of needless paper work. By virtue of the new procedure under the proposed amendments the security given at the outset will be security for the payment of all loans and advances made or to be made under the seasonal line of credit granted under the original and any supplementary applications for credit and promises to give security. Property of the kind assigned whether' owned or to be owned by the borrower is covered, thus facilitating the operation of a revolving line of credit and covering raw materials as they are acquired and manufactured. The
Bank Act-Mr. Ilsley

security will therefore conform to manufacturing and other business methods and will operate, in effect, as a continuing security, simplifying the process of giving security.
The result, it is obvious, will be to reduce the great amount of work required of customers who continue acquiring new property upon which they wish to borrow money. At the present time a grain dealer, for instance, who has already applied for and been granted a line of credit for the season and has signed a promise to give security may have to complete and sign daily not only a promissory note but a fresh assignment under section 88, describing all the promissory notes to be covered as well as the property covered and the place or places in which it is located. Under the new procedure an application for credit for the season coupled with a promise to give security will be signed. When funds are required, security in the new form will be given which will suffice for the season and as additional funds are needed all that will be necessary for the borrower to do will be to give covering promissory notes pursuant to the application for the seasons's credit. Consequently it is claimed that what has of a number of branches and it is sometimes previously been accomplished through a most laborious and cumbersome procedure both for borrowers and bank staffs will be accomplished with a minimum of effort and at the same time the banks will not be getting any thing in the way of security that they are not now getting for the same revolving credit as a result of the present laborious procedure.
It will be obvious to the house that these changes while primarily procedural, are nevertheless of real importance. The opportunity which the committee will have of crossquestioning w'itnesses from both business and banks will, I believe, enable hon. members to determine whether the greater convenience to the business community and the more readily availability of credit under section 88 warrant the adoption of these proposals. I am prepared to be guided by the views which the committee will reach upon the basis of the evidence.
I shall omit any reference to other minor changes and proceed immediately to explain the most important and I believe the most constructive changes which we are suggesting in this banking bill. I refer to the proposals designed to make credit, particularly intermediate credit, readily available on reasonable terms to farmers and fishermen.
In the field of agricultural credit the primary function of the chartered banks in the past has been to provide short-term or seasonal loans to farmers for the financing of current production. The widespread system of branches

which our Canadian banks have established has on the whole proved well adapted to a country of great distances and rapidly changing frontiers of settlement. To facilitate farm lending, section 88 has been amended from time to time during the past fifty years, with the result that it is uniquely adapted to Canadian agricultural conditions, there being no counterpart so far as I am aware in any other country. Under this section loans can be made to farmers for any purpose on the security of threshed grain and livestock, and for the purchase of seed, fertilizer and binder twine on the security of the growing crop.
These provisions of the Bank Act have enabled the banks to extend credit on an extensive scale to farmers for the growing, harvesting and marketing of their crops. Nevertheless, there has been criticism both of the banks and of the legislation. The most common complaint is that the banks have been unduly restrictive in their lending policy, particularly during periods of difficulty such as were experienced during the drought and depression years of the thirties. This is a matter of judgment and I hold no brief for the bankers, who will have an opportunity to answer for themselves before the banking and commerce committee. There has also been criticism of the banks as a result of the closing said that with the smaller number of branches the banks are now unable to give adequate service to farmers in certain areas. It seems to me, however, that the credit stringency during the thirties and the closing of branches in rural areas were in the main a reflection of the unsatisfactory situation then prevailing in agriculture, due in part to drought and other climatic hazards and in part to the effect of the world-wide depression on agricultural prices. The government has already done much, and proposes to do more, for the purpose of achieving reasonable stability in agricultural incomes. As a nation, we must, and we are determined to, achieve a better balance between our rural and our urban economies and even without the legislation which the government has announced for establishing a floor under the prices of the major agricultural products, it seems to me that the outlook .for the agricultural industry in the years immediately following the war will be more promising than it has been in a very long time. Given any reasonable assurance of stable prices and agricultural prosperity, I do not think that farmers will have any difficulty in securing from the banks the credit they need to finance their shortterm or seasonal requirements. It also seems to me the reasonable expectation that the banks will only be too ready to re-open

Bank Act-Mr. Ilsley
branches in any community where there is any prospect of the branches being selfsustaining.
At the other end of the scale are the longterm credit requirements of agriculture. I need hardly remind the house that the chartered banks are not empowered under the Bank Act to lend on the security of real estate mortgages. This has been a fundamental principle of Canadian banking since confederation and experience has, I think, proved its soundness for depositors, borrowers and shareholders alike. The long-term credit needs of agriculture therefore, must be and are being met by a different set of institutions, namely, the insurance companies, the mortgage and loan companies and government lending agencies which specialize in mortgage lending. In this field the dominion' has acted directly not only by making long-term mortgage loans available to war veterans, both after the last war and now under the new and generous Veterans Land Act, but also to other farmers through the Canadian farm loan board. I have already referred to the Central Mortgage Bank Act which was intended to facilitate lending by private agencies in this field, but the operation of which had to be postponed for the time being. Although in the meantime there has been a very substantial reduction in farm debts throughout Canada, it would be a mistake to assume that the need for a central mortgage institution has disappeared and, as I have already intimated, parliament may soon wish to give reconsideration to this legislation, perhaps with an approach somewhat different from that required by the special problems confronting us in 1939.
There remains for consideration another field of farm credit which grows steadily in importance as standards of living rise on the farms and as mechanization of the farm proceeds. This is the kind of credit needed by farmers to increase the efficiency of their farming operations and to add to the amenities of life on the farm. Loans for such purposes would usually be required for from two or three years to eight or ten years and are therefore usually referred to as intermediate credit. Such loans have not ordinarily been available from the banks partly because of the limitations imposed by the Bank Act, and partly because, as the liabilities of the banks are mostly in the form of deposits withdrawable on demand or short notice, it has always been thought desirable that they should keep their assets in rather liquid form. On the other hand, the farmer seldom feels justified in raising money for these purposes from a mortgage institution.
The Canadian Farm Loan Act provided for a system of intermediate credit by making second mortgage loans available for the purpose of consolidating debts, purchasing stock, machinery and equipment and making permanent improvements, but as such loans could be made only to farmers who were also borrowers on first mortgage from the board, these particular facilities were of course available to relatively few farmers. In the main, intermediate credit of this type has been provided to farmers by the implement companies, lumber dealers and other manufacturers and merchants with something durable or semidurable to sell to the farmer. Financing of this kind is always relatively costly, partly because it is not sufficiently selective and partly because the farmer obtains his credit not directly but at second hand. One of the greatest difficulties was that the good farmer, able and willing to pay his debts on the dot, had to bear the burden of the losses and heavy collection costs caused by the inefficient or irresponsible farmer who could not or would not pay his debts as they came due. I have heard it said that a not inconsiderable portion of the cost of farm implements is due to the loading included in the price to take care of the losses and the high collection costs incurred by the implement companies. The term and method of repayment of these trade credits are also usually standardized and frequently are not adapted to the special circumstances of individual farmers. I think the house will agree that, if we can establish a workable system under which the farmer can pay cash to the manufacturer or dealer for his machinery and equipment and secure from some other source a credit on reasonable terms and with repayment adapted to his probable income receipts, we shall be making a real contribution to the reduction in the price of farm machinery and equipment and to the efficient and economical conduct of the farming industry.
I think also there can be little doubt of the extent of the need. With the shortage of man-power and materials, farm equipment and farm buildings must have been allowed to rim down during the war years. When the war ends and controls are relaxed, there will presumably be need for an extensive reequipment programme for Canadian agriculture. Moreover, as part of a programme of post-war reconstruction and in order to improve farm efficiency and the amenities of farm life, we will wish to see a wide extension of rural electrification and widespread activity in the repair, renovation and construction of farm buildings. We will wish to see better houses, as well as better bams, and more bathrooms, more elec-
Bank Act-Mr. Ilsley

trie stoves, and more electric refrigerators in our farm homes. Finally, there will always be need for intermediate credit for drainage and fencing, for building up herds of live stock and for other permanent improvements.
Granted the need, how is credit for these purposes to be made readily available to farmers? Serious consideration over a long period of time has been given to various aspects of this problem. For a time we felt that we might have to set up a new government institution, perhaps somewhat similar to the proposed industrial development bank, with a hierarchy of offices and agencies throughout the country. The house will appreciate, however, that unlike the industrial development bank which will operate with a relatively few offices and a comparatively small but highly skilled staff, a similar agency to provide intermediate credit for agriculture could only do its job effectively with literally thousands of branches or offices throughout rural areas readily accessible to farmers. Some of the United States farm credit organizations were considered as possible models, but the government did not feel justified in imposing on farm borrowers, or on the country as a whole, the additional burden which the overhead costs of such an extensive organization would involve when the same objective could be attained more speedily and effectively and at a fraction of the cost by a comparatively simple extension of existing lending facilities. Moreover, a new set of institutions would have taken years to build up and to equip with competent and experienced staff. In contrast the solution which we are proposing offers facilities already at hand, ready to start to work to-morrow if we should decide that the public need so requires.
That solution is based on certain enactments which will make it possible for the chartered banks to supply the intermediate credit needs of agriculture, and which will encourage them to supply those needs to the fullest possible extent and upon reasonable terms and conditions. In the bill now before you, you will find a number of provisions enabling the banks to make the loans required and to take appropriate security therefor. The government proposes to introduce a companion measure to be called "The Farm Improvement Loans Act" which, if enacted, will authorize the Minister of Finance to give limited guarantees to banks in respect of loans made to farmers for specified purposes and complying with specified conditions, much along the lines of the old Home Improvement Loans Act which had such a successful experience in the years just prior to the outbreak of war.

If the house will bear with me, I shall endeavour to explain my proposals in somewhat greater detail. The enabling provisions in the Bank Act are to be found in paragraphs (f), (g) and (h) of subsection 1 of section 88 and in subsections 2 and 3 of section 89. These provisions enable loans to be made to farmers for the purchase of agricultural implements upon the security of such agricultural implements for the purchase or installation of agricultural equipment or a farm electric system (defined to include all machinery, apparatus and appliances for the generation or distribution of electricity on a farm) upon the security of such agricultural equipment or farm electric system, whether movable or affixed; and for permanent improvements generally upon the security of agricultural implements. Permanent improvements in this sense will include the alteration or improvement of a farm electric system, the erection or construction of fencing or drainage works, the construction, repair, alteration or extension of any building or structure on a farm, and any other works for the improvement or development of a farm for which a farm improvement loan may be made under the companion legislation.
The provisions to ensure that these facilities will be made available to farmers to the fullest possible extent, at reasonable rates of interest and for sufficiently long terms will be found in the collateral measure to which I have referred. It would not be appropriate for me on this occasion to explain in detail the terms of that measure which is not yet before the house. However, to enable hon. members to grasp the significance of the changes being made in the Bank Act, I may be permitted to refer to some of its general principles. It will authorize the Minister of Finance to guarantee a bank against loss up to a specified proportion of the aggregate amount of loans of the eligible category made by a bank; incidentally it is intended that this specified proportion shall be 10 per cent. The bill will specify the types of loans that will be eligible for this guarantee. They will be classified by purpose and type of security to be taken, and the length of term as well as the maximum amount of loan permitted will vary with the class of loan. The maximum interest rate allowed to be charged by the banks will be 5 per cent simple interest per annum. There will of course be a limit on the total amount of loans which may be guaranteed without further enactment by parliament as well as a limit on the amount of loan which may be made in respect of any one farm. Finally, the legislation will permit the guarantee of loans not only to farmers who own their own farms

Bank Act-Mr. Ilsley
but, also for certain types of purposes, to purchasers under agreements for sale and tenant farmers as well.
It is obvious that this direct and simple approach to the problem of intermediate credit for agriculture has several very important advantages. It avoids delay; the loans can be made available throughout farm areas the day after the legislation comes into effect. It avoids the hazards and the additional costs of building up an elaborate, new and untried bureaucratic organization. It affords a desirable combination of government assistance with business judgment. The banks will be encouraged by the government guarantee to make loans wherever there is a reasonable prospect of repayment, yet they will retain sufficient interest in the soundness of each loan to exercise ordinary business prudence. Any cost which may ultimately have to be borne by the government should not be large in relation to the great benefits which will accrue The principle has already been applied with conspicuous success in the home improvement plan, the banks lending $50 million to home owners, mostly in urban districts, and within a period of two or three years. Under that plan of government guarantee, the losses to date are only about three-quarters of one per cent.
These new facilities for short and intermediate term agricultural credit form another and important part of the government's programme to prepare the way for a high level of employment and income after the war. The benefits will be available in some measure as soon as the legislation comes into effect, but the full value will appear only when wartime restrictions are lifted.

During the war some farmers will have accumulated funds to pay for their own post-war programmes, but it is essential that such additional financing as may be necessary and desirable should be available on terms that do not place an undue burden on the farmer. This is particularly important in view of the necessary replacements that must take place when supplies of implements and equipment are again available in full volume. I may add that the government is hopeful that these new facilities will be used extensively in the improvement, modernization and electrification of farm homes which, I am convinced, should be one of this country's major post-war objectives.
Our study of the special credit needs of agriculture led to an examination of the credit needs of other primary industries. Facilities of section 88 of the Bank Act have been available for a long time to the logger and the lumber man, and I know of no difficulty in this field which would suggest the need of any special legislation at this time. There are, however, real and difficult problems in the fishing industry.

speechtext:
This industry presents problems not only in the credit field but in the economic and social fields as well. Provision of better credit facilities will be helpful but will of course not solve all the problems. Conditions as between the Pacific coast, Atlantic coast and inland fisheries vary considerably, but the need for new capital is probably greatest along the Atlantic coast where fishing is carried on in scattered communities originally adapted to salt fish production which have only recently begun to
Bank Act-Mr. Ilsley

adjust themselves to modern conditions of freezing and canning. It is significant that ninety per cent of the fishermen on the Atlantic coast work on their own account. Most of these fish in the coastal waters from small boats which cannot put to sea except in good weather. Deep sea fishing is organized on a large-scale basis and is carried on chiefly by corporations owning a number of boats or by co-operative groups, fishermen and others, who join together in the ownership and operation of a vessel. Low prices and relative depression in the industry from 1928 to 1939 prevented individual fishermen from accumulating any surplus themselves. For the same reasons outside funds were not attracted to the industry in any volume. The mortgage lending institutions found it difficult to do business with fishermen because of the lack of substantial collateral. Consequently, fishermen working on their own account have had to rely often on instruments made by hand or on the cheapest type of capital goods such as might be provided by merchants or outfitters on credit. In recent years credit unions in certain districts and the fishermen's loan board in Nova Scotia have supplanted merchants as a source of capital, but the resources of these institutions allow them to make relatively small loans. In only a comparatively few localities have fishermen been doing business with commercial banks. In short, although fishermen are more prosperous now than for many years, the credit facilities at the disposal of the fishing industry are incapable of providing the capital for that improvement and increase in efficiency of boats and gear and processing equipment which will be necessary if the industry is to be reasonably prosperous after the war. Only through such increase in efficiency can our fish resources be exploited effectively and the highly perishable product handled in such a way as to compete with modern food industries.
The Industrial Development bank should be useful in meeting some of the capital requirements of the fishing industry as its powers include the granting of credit for the construction of fishing craft or for refrigeration or other processing needs. In order to permit and encourage the chartered banks to finance at least certain of the short-term and intermediate credit needs of fishermen, we are proposing an amendment to section 88 of the Bank Act which would make it possible for a bank to make loans to any fisherman upon the security of fishing vessels, fishing equipment and supplies or upon the catch itself.
To make these provisions fully effective, it will be necessary, I believe, to enact a companion measure somewhat similar to the Farm

Improvement Loans Act which I have already described, which will enable the government to give a limited guarantee in respect of loans made by chartered banks to fishermen. It will probably not be possible to introduce this legislation at the current session of parliament. Other measures will have to be taken by government to enable this industry to become a healthfully functioning industry providing reasonable economic returns and sound social conditions and all these measures must fit together into a well rounded and integrated programme for the industry as a whole. A careful investigation is being undertaken with this objective in view. In the meantime it is proposed that loans made by banks for the renovation or modernization of the homes of fishermen, many of whom in fact combine fishing with farming or logging, may be included under the guarantee facilities to be provided for under housing legislation to be introduced later.
I have now completed this long survey of the major changes which we are proposing in our banking legislation as well as of the considerations and guiding principles with which we approached this decennial revision. I trust that the house will agree that we have made a very serious effort to bring this legislation up to date and to make sure, in so far as it can be done by legislation, that our banking system will meet efficiently and effectively the varying requirements of the different sections of our population and thereby make the maximum contribution to the building and development of the greater and better Canada to which we all look forward.
On motion of Mr. Ilsley the debate was adjourned.

speechtext: The house resumed from Monday, May 1, consideration in committee of a resolution to grant to His Majesty certain sums of money for the carrying out of measures consequent upon the existence of a state of war-[DOT] Mr. Ilsley-Mr. Bradette in the chair.
National selective service programme, $11,002,429.

At
page 560 of Hansard the hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy) is reported as follows:
The point is that these people object to paying for the war under compulsion. One of these

War Appropriation-Labour
men tells me that if he had consented to pay $2 a week to the Red Cross he could have avoided going to gaol or going into the army.
Who made that statement? I never did.
The hon. member for York South.
I am not responsible for any statement made by him. You had better ask him the question.

The hon. member asked the minister of defence a question in that regard, and I wondered whether there was any truth in it because a number of people have asked me the same question. Does the minister say that there is no truth in it?

I am dealing with a
man-power pool of 1,600,000 people. I cannot answer offhand a question of that kind, but I doubt whether there is any substantiation for the statement that a man in exchange for $2 a week to some organization can escape going to gaol. To me it does not ring true.
The statement is, going to gaol or into the army. It is something that should be cleared up.

In this regard, I asked the minister a question about conscientious objectors and particularly the number of conscientious objectors who are allowed to remain on the farms of parents or relatives and do their alternative service on these farms. I have in mind a man who was declared a conscientious objector and who was given certain forms to be executed. In those forms there was a clause whereby, as long as $15 a month was paid to the Red Cross, this man was guaranteed the right to remain on the farm, but if the employer failed to turn over $15 a month, in that event the man was to be sent to an alternative camp. That is as recently as March 21 of this year. The minister said that he did not like to see men sent to these camps because the work they would do would not be necessary to the war effort. I have before me a copy of the agreement which conscientious objectors working on farms are required to sign. One provision is that the employer shall pay for the employee's services in respect of such employment at the rate of farm labour, $40 per month, and the employer shall further provide suitable board and lodging for the employee. The employer shall pay to the employee the sum of $25 per month. The employer shall pay to the Canadian Red Cross Society, or such person as the Minister of Labour may designate to
receive the same for the Canadian Red Cross Society, the balance of said monthly payment payable by the employer for the employee's services, namely, the sum of $15 per month.
How many of the 8,000 conscientious objectors now on farms are actually on farms of their parents or brothers? As regards the Doukhobors, the minister says that the problem has been completely solved in Saskatchewan. What it amounts to in their case is the approval of the flouting of these regulations by these people. I should like the minister to give the numbers with regard to these people, and then I have something more to say in that connection.

I have not the figures in front of me of the people on their own farms. I shall be glad to look up that information and find out the disposition of these people if it is physically possible. Let me be frank about this; I still hold the opinion that it is far better to have these people working in a productive capacity than to have them tucked away in some camp, provided they comply with the law. If they do not comply with the law they go into a camp. Make no mistake about that.

What it amounts to is this: while alternative service was prescribed and the method of that alternative service was described, the result to-day is that for the payment of $15 a month to the Red Cross these people are allowed to perform service on behalf of others on their own relatives' farms.
There is another matter I should like to ask the minister about because it is of considerable importance. It has not been answered because it has not been drawn to the minister's attention. This information is of great importance in discussing the minister's speech because it has to do with the availability of reinforcements for the armed services. In his speech the minister used these words, which are to be found at page 2445 of Hansard:
Recently my colleague, the Minister of National Defence (army), made the statement in the house that he would require 60,000 men in the year commencing the first of April. In further correspondence with me, he has stressed the absolute necessity of obtaining these men, particularly bearing in mind the requirements of operations which are in prospect. In the last six months, September, 1943, to February, 1944, there actually have been more than 5,000 men per month who were enlisted and enrolled in the army alone. However, the monthly average has been decreasing, and at times enlistments and enrolments have fallen below the numbers required by the army.
This is a matter upon which the minister must have full statistics. At page 2445 of Hansard I asked him the question as to the
War Appropriation-Labour

months when the numbers enlisted and enrolled fell below the numbers required. As I understand it the difference between the enlistments and enrolments is that enlistment represents volunteering for service anywhere and enrolment represents the recording of a man's callup in the home defence army. I ask the minister to give the figures as to the numbers that have been asked for by the Minister of National Defence for the army in each of the months beginning October 1, last, and also the numbers required under the call-up scheme from month to month, and the degree to which these requirements have been met month by month to date. The minister said that he had the information available but did not have it before him at the moment. The minister said, as reported at page 2445 of Hansard:
I can get those figures for my hon. friend, but I think he will appreciate that when you are operating machinery of the magnitude I am, you cannot remember all these little details. I shall be glad to make a note and get those figures at the earliest opportunity.
I ask the minister to furnish that information now.

That still stands, Mr. Chairman. I will get the figures. I have them here in a partial way. Since my hon. friend has been talking figures I intend to talk figures. I intend to talk about this phantom army of
390,000	people in respect of which my hon. friend made the headlines as usual this morning.

The
minister will make them to-morrow morning.

I do not think so. The newspapers in which my hon. friend made the headlines are not newspapers that are friends of this government. My hon. friend made the same mistake as was made last year and there is a simple explanation for it. I should like to draw to his attention the situation with respect to the province of Quebec, to which he referred. He said that there were only 8,872 called up when there should have been 39,000.
Mr. DIEFENBAIvER: Called up for medical examination in military district F.

Wait until I am through. I think he told only half the story and he put the worst possible complexion on that half. He is assuming the total number called to report for medical examination at Quebec is the total number called in the province of Quebec. He has simply omitted the total number called to report in the city of Montreal. The total for the two , places is 81,855, just about ten times as many as my hon. friend mentioned in his speech yesterday.

In dealing with man-power figures I do not wonder that one becomes confused. They are, of course, big figures. May I refer to table No. 7, which was placed on Hansard on April 28 and may be found at page 2451. An explanation of the accounting has been made there and shows a total of 1,665,504. It is not exact. I am frank to admit it is not exact accounting because there is an additional shortage of 49,000 men, and not
390,000	men, as my hon. friend pointed out yesterday. I am confident that when I next make a survey of the man-power resources of this country before this committee we shall have been able to account for the 49,000 men. May I say that there are deficiencies in every country where there is a man-power problem. It is inevitable. People die and you do not know anything about them. In the Dominion of Canada people slip across the border and join the United States army; they go into the mercantile marine, and so on, but I do not think it is in the best interests of Canada to broadcast figures of that kind, because after all is said and done, the 390,000 men of whom my hon. friend speaks constitute almost as big a number as the total of the active forces, army, of the Dominion of Canada. I think the people of this country, and even the hon. member himself, take that figure with a grain of salt. He is simply taking the number of orders to report for medical examination and deducting the number of men who reported. The remainder he calls the "lost men". If you look at the table appearing at page 4039 of Hansard of 1943 you will see that there is an explanation of the difference, and it is a simple explanation.
Then my hon. friend takes order No. 142-A, which shows the result of the military training call-up as of January 31, 1944. This shows 433,453 men called, and it explains just what happened. It admits that 9,274 who were called did not comply, and, in addition, that 4,803 orders did not reach the men, making a total of 14,077 as of January 31, 1944. These have not been located, but we have been tracing them and some of them have, of course, been located since that date. Instead of using the figure 14,077, my hon. friend adds another 5,000, making a total of 19,077. I am afraid my hon. friend did not study arithmetic in the same school that I did.
That is true.
At page 2498 of Hansa/d my hon. friend speaks of 22,000 men having been found by commission agents. Actually the figure is 25,710.

The figure given
by the minister the other day was 22,000.

War Appropriation-Labour

I said that was an
approximate figure. I have a vivid recollection of that; I was very careful about it, because I was making an extended statement at that time. I pointed out very clearly to my hon. friend that the figure was approximate. Again on the same page the hon. gentleman speaks of the total number of prosecutions up to the end of March, 1944, as being 4,214, when actually there were 5,227.

Was that not the
correct number up to the end of January?

No; the total was 5,227. If I may put it in this way, I do not think it is quite the right thing to endeavour to place other than a proper interpretation upon the man-power situation of this country. It is like the case of a man biting a dog; that is news, while it is not news if a dog bites a man. I do not consider it quite right to let the story go to the four corners of the earth that we have 390,000 men missing as far as the call-up is concerned. Last year it was the man-power muddle; this year I suppose it is going to be the lost battalion. Before hon. gentlemen make statements of that kind, if they are not clear on the facts my office is always open, as are the offices of my officials. If hon. gentlemen want to place the correct interpretation upon any figures dealing with such a vital question as the man-power situation of this country, I am sure my office door always swings both ways, as well as the doors of the offices of my officials provided the information solicited is of a kind that can be made public without being of any assistance to the enemy.

May I ask the minister
if the figures coming from his office would be at all different from the figures given in the house?

Of course not; why
should they be?

I do not know, but I
understood that the hon. member had built his case upon the figures contained in a return brought down in the house.

The same mistake was
made last year, and I assume that my hon. friends went back to the computation they made at that time. I have sat in opposition in this house; I think I know the duties of an opposition. As I said the other day, when you are asking a question you may spend hours in drafting it so as at least to make it difficult for the government, if not actually embarrassing. So it is when you deal with a set of figures: sometimes when your case is not very good you will not make the sort of
computation you would make if you were sitting where I am, and had to give the Canadian people the figures as they exist in my department. I am not going to say more than that, Mr. Chairman, except that I hope the press to-morrow will make the necessary corrections, not necessarily in the interests of any political party but in the interests of this dominion and the war effort it has been making since the outbreak of hostilities.

Now the minister
has stated his side of the story it becomes necessary for me to present the figures which I did not place upon Hansard yesterday, and all of which came from the minister's office. I do so because, while the minister has not attempted any explanation of the lost individuals to whom I referred, yesterday afternoon, as reported at page 2501 of Hansard, said:
My hon. friend spoke about figures . . . I do not want to take him too harshly to task on that, but I think that observation might be made in reverse, and I say that in a kindly way. I mean the figures my hon. friend quoted were all staggered.
I take it that the meaning of those words was that the figures I gave dealt with different periods. The figures I gave yesterday- they are in the returns office and can be checked there-all had to do with the period up to January 31, 1944. There would be no necessity for me to place these figures upon Hansard, if instead of returns being brought down which find their way to the returns office and there remain embalmed, the answers to the questions asked by hon. members in connection wiht such matters were placed upon Hansard itself. Let me begin with the statement by the minister that I was in error when I stated that 22,000 represented the number who had been prosecuted.
Not 22,000 prosecuted.
That 22.000 had been picked up.
No, not even picked up; traced.
When I made my speech yesterday afternoon I was relying upon the figures which had been given me by the minister the day before, but they were revised and enlarged after I spoke.
My hon. friend will admit-
I did not interrupt the minister.

That is all very well, but I do not want to be accused of bad faith. I was making a lengthy statement; my hon.
War Appropriation-Labour

friend asked me a question and I said that I had not the figures before me but that these were the approximate figures.

Now I am criticized for having relied upon the approximate figures given by the minister. Yesterday the figure was revised up to 25,000. The approximate figure given the day before, upon which I relied, was 22,000, and I am now to be criticized for having used the figures given to parliament by the minister. I think that is sufficient on that point.
Then the minister said I was in error as to the number of prosecutions. In that regard I was relying upon return No. 142F, in which figures were asked as to prosecutions against defaulters under the National Resources Mobilization Act up to January 31, 1944, the last figures available, by provinces or military districts. They are not dodgers; I would not go that far.

It is amazing the number of young men who are believed to be dodgers of service with the armed forces.
If three per cent only are missing who are not even dodgers, that would not be amazing. The statement made by Mr. Butler indicates how widespread and how great is the number of those who have disappeared. The record tells its own story. I now pause for a moment to answer a statement made a moment ago by the minister.
Where did you get that last figure? It must be from some other return.

It is the same return, No. 142E, showing the number of men who reported for medical examination on January 31, 1944. The reason why we have to ask for this information in two different questions is so that we would get the exact figures, of the same date, namely, January 31, 1944. When information on call-ups is given as it used to appear in "Canada at War", we were enabled to analyse the statements as changes from month to month took place. Then a new system of bookkeeping was set up. So that in order to get the information, we have to follow the course of asking questions at different times, but as of a given date-not as of different dates.
I paused a moment ago to answer what the minister had said. He said I had made a statement which was not in acccordance with the facts, so far as district F at Quebec is concerned. The statement I made was that fewer than 9,000 of the number called up for medical examination between June 23, 1943, and January 31, 1944, came from district F, Quebec. I did not mention Montreal. It had a very large call-up for medical examinations. I mentioned Quebec district only, and here are the figures: Military district F, Quebec, number of men called up for medical examination as of January 31, 1944, 116,607. So that the statement I made was entirely correct. And it is borne out by the figures given by the minister last June, and the return, No. 142A.
I now proceed to the next figure. Some of the disappeared group enlisted, on receipt of the order. That leaves a further number of 141,000 who are still lost and who still must be accounted for.
How many does that make altogether?

They can be totalled up. These are not staggered figures; these are figures that come from different returns and they are reinforced by what is shown in "Canada at War". "Canada at War" issued full figures in January and February, 1943, which revealed the situation and showed the trend that was taking place. Men were disappearing and enforcement was falling down. We in the opposition drew that matter to the attention of the country. What happened? Those figures did not appear again in "Canada at War" throughout 1943.
In January, 1944, we had a new set of figures and a new basis of bookkeeping in "Canada at War". It is only by an examination of returns such as I have referred to-I have taken all of the particulars in those returns that have anything at all to do with the matter-that we find out the position of affairs. In spite of the fact that the minister would wave the situation aside there has been no explanation of where these men are, what happened to them or what is taking place in connection with enforcement.
Yesterday the minister stated that he had nothing to do with the courts of this country. That is quite true. I referred to the extremely low penalties being imposed upon men who have been convicted as defaulters under these regulations. It is true that the minister has no control over the courts, but he can alter the penalties that are provided for in the regulations and make the punishment such that those who are minded to default will realize that there is no profit in taking that action.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.

After Recess
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

I think I have now placed before the committee sufficient information from the returns and information furnished by the department itself to establish conclusively that not only were the statements made by me yesterday in accordance with the facts, but that the actual figures disclose an even greater number of delinquents than were referred to by me. I have set out in detail, based on the various sessional papers which have been brought down, the number of men to whom medical notices were sent, the number who reported in pursuance thereof, and finally the number who were called up for military service and the very considerably lower number who reported; and deducting therefrom the numbers shown to have enlisted, and the statutory exemptions, the figures I gave yesterday, I repeat, have been conclusively proven. They cannot be answered by merely saying, "Well, we cannot explain the shortage; or the loss, or the missing hundreds of thousands; they must be around, they must be in the armed services"; for I would point out that the department has very full records to-day. Last Friday the minister showed that the number of people in the armed services of Canada and at work was 5,057,000, being fifty-seven per cent of those fourteen years and over. Last year the figures he gave were that the number in the category fourteen years and over was 8,720,000. The government Las the records. The answers regarding man-power given to the house have been summarized by me and brought together in a composite picture; and they reveal exactly the situation to which I referred yesterday.
Another matter to which I wish to refer is that of medical fitness. There is a pronounced difference in the degrees of medical fitness in the various provinces; and I should like to know from the minister whether the Pulhems system for the medical examination of recruits or of those called up under the National Resources Mobilization Act is being used in every province, or whether its application is confined to one or more provinces.
It is used in all the provinces.

So that it is being used everywhere across the dominion? Its application no doubt accounts for the very large percentage of men who are found to be physically unfit. Now that I have the assurance of the minister in that regard I need not pursue the matter any further.

There is just one other point I wish to make. I referred this afternoon to the January, 1943, issue of " Canada at War." I should like to refer to the February, 1943, issue of the same publication, which showed the position of affairs in so far as the call-up is concerned to December 26, 1942. Even at that time it was admitted in the particulars which were given that 87,485 medical examination notices had been undelivered, that 9,345 military training notices had been undelivered, and that in addition there were cases pending and delinquent and otherwise unaccounted for, numbering 98,128. According to the official records, therefore, the number unaccounted for, including cases pending, was then 194,958. Today the situation is much more serious. The number has rapidly increased until it now amounts to the figures I gave yesterday. What I ask of the minister is the latest figures on the situation. The question was asked yesterday by the hon. member for Hastings-Peterborough, who requested a recapitulation of the figures up to date in order to show the proper, unvarnished position so that the Canadian people might know the facts.
I have given the facts revealed by the answers of the minister and the returns brought down in this house. Those figures, startling as they are. cannot be answered by a mere sweep of the arm and a declaration that they are meaningless; they stand as a direct challenge to the government. Yesterday I placed before this house and the country the generalizations based on the information furnished to this house in the returns; to-day I have supported my statements by figures directly and definitely taken from the government's own answers. The responsibility now is upon the government to meet the situation.
I again suggest that enforcement is important and that it can never be achieved while the penalties provided for under the regulations are of so low an amount that they actually operate as an invitation to those who would be delinquent to continue to be so; for if a man escapes for two, three, four or five months and the only penalty imposed upon him is a twenty-five dollar fine, there is an invitation to wrongdoing, for the penalty is not comparable with the offence.
A j'ear or so ago, there were many who did not understand the regulations, and the provisions for the penalties at that time could be justified. Everybody knows the regulations to-day. Every newspaper in Canada has carried advertisements. Not only that, but a check-up has been taking place all the time. In addition, immunity was offered; all who would return would be forgiven. Yet in the face of all these activities Mr. Butler in Toronto was justified in indicating recently that the situation was appalling in its result. And the minister takes my remarks as a personal criticism. Far from it; it is not given in that way. It is a situation which is difficult. The responsibility was placed on him; he started with an inheritance of delinquents, but that inheritance has been increased.
All we ask is that this condition be frankly faced. To-day we are short of man-power: the minister says that his department is scraping the bottom of the barrel. If so, surely now is the time, having regard to the fact that we face the darkest period of the war in so far as prospective casualties are concerned, to secure the mobilization of every available man. Now is the time to have revealed to the country the situation as shown by the returns referred to, to the end that an intensified campaign may be undertaken with a view to securing the necessary man-power. Placing this matter, not on the basis of any hypothesis, not on anything but the figures of the government, I do not think the minister has any right to suggest that the figures I have given are not in accordance with the facts. Every statement I made yesterday has been to-day established on the basis of the government's returns. I have given a composite picture of the situation, and I ask the minister now to explain what appears to be up to the present time, so far as the department is concerned, the inexplicable disappearance of hundreds of thousands of men.

If the minister will permit me before he replies to the hon. member, I have some observations to make, as one who is in daily contact with the soldiers and with the draftees. My hon. friend the member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) is one of the best debaters in this house and I regret profoundly that the figures he has quoted do not speak as well as he does himself.

speechtext: Not half so eloquent.

There are many things to consider in connection with this problem, and I will not insist on his quotation of what Mr. James Butler, the chief investigating officer of the Toronto Branch of the mobilization board, said according to the Toronto Telegram of March 4, 1944:
It is amazing the number of young men who are said to be dodgers of service *with the armed forces.
While quoting Mr. Butler, my hon. friend rendered a service to his colleagues in this
War Appropriation-Labour

house by informing them that the situation is amazing in Toronto and therefore is bad not only in military district No. 5, Quebec.
I have nothing to say in the matter of complaint against what is happening in Toronto, Quebec or anywhere else, but I want to explain to my hon. friend, if he wishes to know, the reaction of the people, and if he is in contact with his own people as I am with mine he will surely agree with me.
In the first place, I am not at all amazed that the number of young men who were found unfit by military boards was so considerable, because all those who have been classified in category E by their family doctor were called again to pass medical examinations before the army board, and they had been declared unfit before by doctors who had followed them probably since their birth. Those men who were physically unfit, were called again, and they were again in a large number of cases found unfit by the military boards.
In the second place, another class of young men were called to pass their medical test before the army boards. They were those who had secured postponement until further notice, et cetera, from the mobilization board. These were not supposed to enlist.
I am not surprised at all that there is some discrepancy in the figures given by the minister, for this very good reason, that most of those officers, especially those who compose the military boards, are not under the Minister of Labour, but under the Department of National Defence, and therefore he gets his information from the Department of National Defence. I know very well that in Quebec city there is very little cooperation between the registrar and the army medical boards, and it takes a very long time to have a file transferred from one office to another.
Moreover, I do not think my hon. friend is quite as fair as he usually is when he blames the minister for figures that appear in "Canada at War," which is published by the wartime information board under the Prime Minister. We have three branches under three different heads. There is in the first place the Department of National Defence, which is supposed to supply figures to the Department of Labour; then there is the Department of Labour, and then there is the wartime information board. Since it is human to err, I am not surprised that there may be some discrepancy in these figures. I could quote to the hon. gentleman the fact I have mentioned in these last days to the Department of Labour about some young men, seventeen or nineteen in number. They were farmers' sons. They had postponements until further notice, and they went to see the employment officer, selective 
service. They got a permit to work in the forest and they did so. Then, while they were there, they went to the post office, filled in the regular forms, and got receipts. What happened? They were arrested by the mounted police and put on the train. This happened in Ontario. They were put on the train, had handcuffs on them from North Bay to Toronto, and they were sent to various military camps. They were acting in accordance with the law when they were discharging essential duties as farmers and as lumbermen, and it would be impossible for me to argue with my hon. friend if he takes for granted that the army has a priority over essential industry and that those in essential industries are supposed not to do any useful work in this time of war.
That is why I have asked for some detailed information about the essential occupation of men who are not in the army, in order to know what they are really doing for war purposes while working in the forest or on the farm, et cetera, et cetera; and the answers I have received are far from satisfactory.
I will tell my hon. friend more, and my files are at his disposal just as they were at the disposal of the Minister of National Defence. It is that in military district No. 5 the leading officers are not all French Canadian, but I say that in a large number of cases men from my constituency had a Taw deal from the army in that district, a raw deal that they would not have had in another district. Is it fair to penalize military district No. 5 for the incompetency of some officers who are always defended by the Minister of National Defence when he is in the house?
I do not want the Minister of Labour to be made the goat of other departments over which he has no jurisdiction. If he were in charge of all draftees, as he should be, the situation would be entirely different, and the hon. member for Lake Centre would be perfectly justified in arraigning the Minister of Labour and asking him to render an account. But at the present time he knocks at the wrong door. All that he has said to-day should have been said on the estimates of the Department of National Defence. Why should the Minister of Labour be made the goat of the medical boards of the army when these men are not under his jurisdiction? Besides that, this afternoon I listened carefully to my hon. friend, and he said something about conscientious objectors and the Doukhobors. There are quite a lot of conscientious objectors; there are quite a lot of Doukhobors. But I make a great distinction between the man who does not take advantage of that law which is stupid and antiquated and should be repealed, and the others.

War Appropriation-Labour
There is no reason why special treatment should be given to the conscientious objectors, the Mennonites and the Doukhobors. When the plebiscite was before the Canadian people the government asked for a release from all promises made. If the answer "yes" meant that the government was freed of all promises made to the Canadian people it applied as well to Doukhobors, Mennonites and conscientious objectors as to anyone else, and I am one of the very few members who has protested because of such discrimination. It is true that I have in my constituency no Douhkobors, no Mednonites and no conscientious objectors. But if I had I would take the same stand as I do now.
There is something else that my hon. friend should argue on. It is the number of all guests of military age or who have become of military age since they landed in this country from the beginning of the war on We are told that some of them are called now for their military training. Whether that is true or not, I do not know.
It is true.

No statistics have been
given on that point; but this I know, for a time it was supposed to be bad manners to call up any young man who came from some other country and who had reached military age and was in good health. He was not supposed to be called to the army. Here again I ask for the support of the hon. member for Lake Centre. I ask him to support me not only to apply to Mennonites, Doukhobors and conscientious objectors the same treatment as to any other people, but to see to it that every young man of military age when he arrived here or, if he was not of military age, but has become of military age since the beginning of the war and who is in this country, follows the law, respects the law just the same as any other British citizen in this country. I appeal to him for that support.
I appeal to him for another thing. I appeal to him to send overseas as first reinforcements all those pasty youths who are in uniform here in Ottawa, who have never been to any theatre of war and do not intend to go to any theatre of war, who wear the uniform who have allowances at the expense of the Canadian taxpayers, and who are supposed to be heroes just because they wear a uniform. They should be the first to go. I appeal to the hon. member for Lake Centre to support me in urging not only upon the Minister of Labour but upon the government the necessity of putting all these men in the place where they should be. Why should they
wear the uniform like that? Why' should they take up so much space on the sidewalks? Why should they get allowances when they do clerical work? The same with women; they wear the uniform, all right. I have been told very often by the Prime Minister that they were brave, that they were shedding their blood for their country. Let them do so. Let them be brave. Here again I ask for the support of my hon. friend.
I will tell more to my hon. friend. I see my old friend the hon. member for York-Sunbury. He must remember that when his past leader was Prime Minister I very often indulged in statistical work to condemn his government. I spent days and nights in working on figures and numbers of every district about exports and imports, et cetera, et cetera, in order to prove my thesis to condemn the Bennett government. That was in peace time. It is a kind of sport in which I would never indulge in war time, and I regret most profoundly that the hon. member for Lake Centre has been doing in war time precisely the same kind of thing that I had a right to do in peace time, because I was doing that for political purposes and the result was good. It is one of the reasons why my hon. friend was defeated in York-Sunbury, as my speeches were read throughout the land with good effect. But now that we are at war the hon. member for Lake Centre is playing a dangerous game; and when his leader, the late John Bracken-
Oh, oh!

comes to the province of Quebec to make love to the Quebeckers, whether they are French Canadian, Scotch, Irish, English or Jew, he goes. And then after he is gone we hear our friend the hon. member for Lake Centre making speeches such as the one he delivered yesterday and the one he delivered to-day. It will have a very bad effect, and it is not because he mentioned what was said by Mr. James Butler of Toronto about people from Toronto that the people of the province of Quebec will forgive the insult that they have received that they are not doing their duty.
May I tell my hon. friend that I represent a constituency which has supplied the army with perhaps the largest number of men that any rural county has given? I shall not quote many names, but not long ago an officer was honoured here on the occasion of the opening of the sixth victory loan campaign; he was honoured not only here but in many other parts of this country. He was a native son of Temiscouata. Then there
