were many others who were made prisoners at Hong Kong or who were killed at Dieppe, Sicily and many other places.
He left there a long time ago, before you came around.
What does my hon. friend Bay?
I said that he left there before you appeared on the scene.
Would my hon. friend be kind enough to repeat the sublime word?
I will not bother.

I will tell my hon. friend that when he does for the soldiers what I have been doing in my constituency he will have the right to speak to me, and when Filip Konowal, V.C., kisses his hand, as he has kissed mine, he will have the right to speak to me. Until then he should put live charcoal on his mouth. I will not stand for any joke because the people of my constituency have done their duty. I do not care what is said about me. I attach no importance to what the hon. gentleman might say in a derisive way. I tell him that I will be a tiger to defend my own people as they deserve to be defended. I will tell not only my own people; soon I may have an opportunity to tell the people of this province of Ontario how some Tories jeer when we talk of men of whom the country is so proud, men who have done their duty, who have not been afraid to go to war, and who have better war records than that of the hon. member for York-Sunbury. What is his military record? It is the same as that of Arthur Meighen, the same as that of all the Tories who have never been to war but who preach conscription in order to encourage the big contractors who want to sell more boots, more uniforms and more food to the soldiers. Canada Packers! The hon. gentleman is this sort of imperialist. He laughs, just as the Tories laughed during the depression when I mentioned the case of the poor settlers who had to make soup from maple leaves, our national emblem. They laugh; but when John Bracken copies to the province of Quebec he does not speak as the hon. member for Lake Centre spoke yesterday and to-day. If John Bracken comes again, however, the people of the province of Quebec will remind him of what has been said yesterday and to-day. They will remember that the former leader of the opposition, a man who was honoured with the confidence of his

former leader, Mr. Bennett, laughed and jeered when I mentioned the heroes of this war-
I did not laugh at the heroes of the war; I was laughing at you. You ought to be in Verdun.

-because they are French Canadians coming from Quebec. That is why hon. gentlemen opposite laugh. I do not know if my hon. friend had the honour of shaking the hand of Major Paul Triquet, V.C.; but when the time came tp honour a man who had one of the finest records of the last war, a man who is doing the dirty work downstairs, the only holder of the Victoria Cross under this roof now that Major Gregg is in Brock-ville, was it the hon. member for York-Sunbury or the hon. member for Lake Centre or the member for Temiscouata who brought that man before the committee on honours and decorations, who wired the victory loan campaign committee that Filip Konowal, V.C., deserved a place on the stand here, and who introduced him to the Prime Minister, the Minister of National Defence and Major Triquet himself? I did it because an older man, a privy councillor, a man with the authority and prestige of the hon. member for York-Sunbury, did not do it. Now let him laugh.
You are a great man.
Who is a great man?
You are.

Oh, no; I do not pretend to be a great man. I give others an opportunity to do the right thing, but when they do not take advantage of the opportunity I have to do it myself. We are hearing now about national unity. Hon. gentlemen opposite say, "Let us be one in this country." One with Tories like that? Never; it is impossible. It is all right; they may cluck, but when they are behind our backs they are treacherous. They say things that offend the pride of proud men, things that are most contemptible because they may affect the future of this country. As a party man I feel that I am rather independent; but there are things I cannot let pass; there are things to which any man whose heart is in the right place cannot listen without being offended. There are disgraceful scenes which one cannot witness without protesting very strongly and deeply.
Let me remind the hon. member for Lake Centre, the hon. member for York-Sunbury and other hon. gentlemen opposite who may be more serious, that at times they have voted with the

War Appropriation-Labour
Cooperative Commonwealth Federation in order that the farmers might receive more money for their products; but when the time came to defend the farmer himself, because the farmer is an asset to the country, they always voted as one against us. Then they will tell of their love for the farmer. If they want me to recite facts I can do so. I can tell the hon. member for-well, the constituency which he will no longer represent after the next election-that every time I and other members of this house have defended the farmers and asked for a postponement of their training, hon. gentlemen opposite have always voted against us. How can they be believed, then, when they say that they are the friends of the farmers and that John Bracken is milking a cow every day? That may be true, and perhaps they themselves are all anxious to milk the cow, but their statements cannot be taken seriously.
This concludes the first part of my observations in reply to the hon. member for Lake Centre. I wanted to say these few words before the minister answered the hon. member. Let me tell the minister that when a living being has two or three heads it is a success at fairs; it is considered a monster. I do not believe any single thing can be carried into effect successfully when it is decided by three heads. There should be only one head. It will be impossible to deal with selective service successfully until the Minister of Labour is in full charge of it. That should be easy, provided no one has an inferiority complex in regard to the imperialists, those men without a country, who think that Canada is just an adjunct of the empire and that all our policies should be decided in and by London. It will not be enough to have all these matters under the direct control, supervision and direction of the Minister of Labour; it will be essential also to decide all matters of war, in the broadest possible sense, according to the Canadian spirit. I will not shock any Tory by saying that. Was it not Mr. Bennett himself who spoke of "Canada first", a policy that was never applied by him? It is a very sound policy; theoretically it is beautiful, and brings cheers from all comers when it is advocated by someone other than my humble self. That is nothing; my point is that the policy of Canada first should be carried out in fact rather than by words.

I am not going to reply at length to the hon. member for Lake Centre. The points he has raised were covered fairly well in my statement to the house and also in what I might call the basic tables I placed on Hansard at that time. "He has arrived at a figure, and I do not know how he arrived at
it, of 380,000. One hon. member raised the ante up to, I believe, 700,000, and if we debate this question long enough everybody in the dominion will be missing, before we are through.

Mr. Chairman, in view of the fact that the speeches this evening have wandered from the actual subject under discussion, may I crave the indulgence of the committee to start at a point even more remote. In the army time is either hanging very heavily on one's hands, or it is a matter of great immediacy. With that excuse I will, if I may, wander slightly.
It is a long time since I have had an opportunity of saying a few words in this house, and I can do so now only from the point of view of the troops overseas to whom it is to be supposed that these drafts, when they are finally obtained, will be sent. The attitude of a great many of the men overseas toward the question of the drafting and training of men in Canada for the defence of Canada and for fighting overseas is that they are not really greatly concerned with it. The opinion of the men is that fundamentally one either wants to fight or one does not. That may not be a popular thing to say, but that is the fundamental fact which I think all of us on both sides of the house might as well bear in mind.
But there can be no question either in their minds or in ours as to the ultimate result of the policy, however it may be applied. If there are not sufficient men who want to fight, at least those who do must not be let down if it is merely a question of sheer man-power. I must confess that it is a bit disturbing, knowing how well and how magnificently volunteers from the province of Quebec have fought in this war, having been with them, to find that a wrong impression should be created by

War Appropriation-Labour
the passage of a resolution such as was passed recently in the legislature of that province. It does a great deal of harm because it is not explained or understood. It does not lead to that complete understanding and sympathy between our fighting men over there which is what we all seek to achieve. However, it is not a thing I can do anything about; it is not what I rose to talk about.
What I wish to speak about, if I may, is the attitude of the troops, their thoughts, their ideas, their hopes as to what eventually lies before them. I cannot in any sense claim to represent them, but I can at least say with complete truth that I am one of them. I have had some small opportunity of knowing what is going on in their minds. It is a long, far cry from Dunkirk to May 1, 1944. Throughout that time we have managed by means of a volunteer system to build up overseas a large combined air, naval and land force from Canada, a portion of which has been tested in battle and not found wanting, and the remainder of which is waiting to go over into that country to which our fathers went in 1914-18.
Some remarks have recently been made in this house about the part played during this time by the people at home. It is not unusual to find men returning from overeas who become a little bitter on the subject of the attitude of civilians at home. That is understandable, but I just want to say this for myself alone. I have been home only a few weeks, but I have had some opportunity of meeting people in various parts of Canada. I want to pay a tribute to the working men and women of Canada, not only for what they have produced but for the way they have unceasingly and uncomplainingly carried on; and to management for the results that they have produced with the labour at hand. But especially I want to pay a tribute to the citizens of Canada for the way in which they have responded to war loans, Red Cross drives and the many other demands made upon their loyalties and emotions. They have responded month after month and have given vast sums of money to back up in a mute way, the only way that so many of them can, the war effort of this country. This is not a government war; this is not a party war; it is a citizens' war. I am glad that as a soldieT I can come home and find my fellow-citizens doing a first-class job on their front. It will be something to tell my comrades overseas.
'Now something about them. During the long wait we perhaps came to be termed the Duke of York's Own more than anything else. Hon. members will remember that the Duke of York had 10,000 men; he marched them
up the hill and he marched them down again. During that period of the defence of Britain, then in the Mediterranean the fighting in .Sicily and Italy and now when they are on the edge of prospects, the hardest burden our men have had to bear, has not been the food conditions; it has not been the living conditions; it has not been even the liquor conditions; it has been something that their relatives here at home are sharing-homesickness. The hardest thing our troops overseas have to bear is the long sustained absence from their home country. But the fact that in spite of that they have been able to retain their sense of responsibility and discipline is, I think, no mean tribute to them.
Somebody asked me the other day what the boys think about the war itself and about the time that is to come after the war. We are encouraged in knowing that all members of this house are united in the ceaseless endeavour which I have witnessed since I have been here, an endeavour which is supported by a tremendous amount of good will through the country, an endeavour which is led by the government, to provide rehabilitation measures which will allow our boys to take their normal places in Canadian life when they come home. They are bucked up by knowing that that is being done, but I would suggest to the government that some direct measure be taken to provide our troops overseas with knowledge of what has been prepared for them and of what as yet is not completed but is under way. Most of us over there are very ignorant on the subject, and it would add to our understanding of what goes on, and also help our morale, if we had a clearer knowledge of what is being prepared.
We know that no matter what measures may be adopted, what laws may be passed in this chamber, what training may be entered into, what money may be provided, unless the general level of employment in this country is high at the time, those measures will inevitably fail of their own weight to provide employment. We know that the basically sound administration by controls and by government direction has ensured the probability of a satisfactory employment situation at the end of the war, and we want to make sure that they continue in so far as it is necessary.
We also feel very strongly that, because our country has made a measurable sacrifice in this war-and it is not by any means over- it would nevertheless be well now to-consider the fact that we should also, perhaps in a minor way but at least in a minor way, make our small contribution in after-war international meetings to prevent a war in the future. I think that is fundamental.
War Appropriation-Labour

Then, too, at the back of the heads of most of us, I think, is the question of a home. Thousands of our men have married overseas; thousands of others are going to, before the war is over. Many of us have been in the army for four and five years; some of us will soon have been in the service for six years; and while I do not know how long the Japanese affair may continue, it is conceivable that many may have been in the services for seven years before they settle down again in this country. In the army there is no home, and home remains still the anchor of the Canadian overseas. Our idea of home is the mental anchor that sustains us. We look forward to having homes when we come back. We want to make sure that the government, the parliament and the people of this country know that.
Therefore it simply sums up then, does it not, to this, that basically we want to take our share in the provision of a general security. We do not ask, I think, anything beyond the opportunity to provide that for ourselves. After all, we are volunteers in a great adventure.	We want to take our part in the
provision of it for all of us. We want to make sure that we have homes to come back to.
I have personally no great optimism as to the outcome of this war. I do not see abroad in the world any great spirit of tolerance and good will among nations. I have seen in this war, and I know I shall see again, the tremendous value of good will between man and man, and this is a great deal. I have seen the British infantry from Northumbria moving up the line, small, hardy men, as their forefathers were, but great men; I have seen the 51st Highlanders-Scots. I have been alongside the United States troops in this war, and I want to say to you, Mr. Chairman, and the committee and this country, that there are no finer fighting men in the field than the Americans. Alongside the French and the others, from this there comes a great comradeship. I hope that this will be felt, too, between the governments, between the peoples who are represented by these governments, so that there may come out of this, if nothing else, a greater patience, tolerance and understanding among ourselves as peoples and among each other, even here.

I want to bring the committee back for a few minutes to the subject of national selective service and the relationship of employee and employer.
I am going to cite a case to the minister, not as a particular instance but to serve as an example for him to give an opinion regarding

its solution as applicable to conditions which exist throughout the country. I think it is well understood that in the case of an employee-I am going to refer to the miners because I am familiar with mining conditions in the Drumheller fields-a man who has quit his job without giving the required seven days' notice is liable under the regulations to a penalty. He must comply with that requirement, and if he does not do so he can be prosecuted.
Now here is a situation where the mine management itself did not comply with the government regulation in this particular respect. One of the mines in the Drumheller field closed down without giving the men the required seven days' notice. They were somewhat deceitful in the action they took. They knew they were going to close down-they notified the men that they would give them at least two weeks' work before the shut-down came about; and further they informed the men that they could not qualify for unemployment insurance until they had been unemployed for nine days. As a result, the men in this mine did not apply for unemployment insurance, and when they went to make application they found that they had not lived up to the required regulations. These men complain that they have been wrongly treated, and that they should receive at least the seven days' pay which the mining company owes them. It is suggested that the only recognition these men can get would be by starting a civil action. That, it seems to me, is not quite the proper thing. I hope that my information is wrong and that the minister will correct me when he answers this question. I seems to me that there should be some regulation vrhereunder the government will prosecute mine owners or mine management and force them to comply with the law, just as they compel employees to comply with the regulations, because some mining companies are deliberately closing down and debarring their men from their rights. I think the minister knows the case to which I refer, because I have communicated it to him by letter, but other cases have been drawn ,to my attention, and in settling this one we might be able to settle the others. Would the minister tell us what can be done in a case of this kind with the mining companies?

On the question of unemployment insurance, of course, the employees have the right to appear before the referees ir>
the district. On the other question, I should like to point out to my hon. friend that it is not a one-way street; if the workman has to give seven days' notice the employer has to do likewise. You cannot have one law for one group of individuals and a

War Appropriation-Labour
different law, dealing with the same subject, for another group; that kind of thing leads to revolution. While I am not intimately acquainted with the case mentioned by my hon. friend, if he will turn the whole matter over to me I shall have our people investigate it and see if we can do anything for these men.

I did write the minister, and I have his acknowledgment signed by himself. Since I wrote about this case, two others have been drawn to my attention. One was up in the Edmonton district, where a mine deliberately closed down without the men receiving any notice at all, and I am informed by some of the employees who have written to me that they are advised that their only recourse is to take civil action. That should not be so, because presumably the mining companies are subject to some regulation in these matters.

We have an enforcement branch which deals all the time with cases like that. All that men in that position have to do is to write to us, and that sets the thing in motion. I shall be glad to get the details, and if the cases are well founded, the necessary action will be taken.

Just as a matter of information, I should like the minister to explain what appears to be a duplication in table No. 7 to which he referred earlier. In item 2 there is listed a total of 138,497 men as unfit in categories "B", "C", "D" and "E". In the next item, unfit for front line, there are included "B", "C", "D" and "E" categories. Does that imply that the 138,000 men in the second item are also included in the third?
Some men are classified as 'B", but in the final examination they turn cut to be "A". There are two sets of cases; one is positive and the other doubtful.

Are those "B", "C", "D" and "E", included in the third item, men who have been reexamined and are not included in the first, found to be of a lower category later? Just what is the point of giving two sets of figures for the same category?
One is on postponement, and the other is not.

I was very much interested in listening to the excellent speech of the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Chambers), and later on I shall have something to say with reference to some of his remarks. We have had a lot of talk about call-ups, but when we hear the Minister of National Defence speak about our volunteer army one wonders why we have the call-ups. We are 100-162
all proud of our volunteer army and what they have done, but we no longer have a volunteer army. What we have now is a call-up for the purposes of forced volunteering. That is really what it amounts to. The minister the other day said that he had never heard anyone either in the house or elsewhere [DOT]suggest that the volunteer army was not a desirable thing. I agree with him; I think it is a very desirable thing. But this is a modern war, as the hon. member for Nanaimo says, and there are no heroics of the old kind that appeal to the people to-day. It is a business, and it is not practical to have volunteers altogether.
The minister said, "I have repeatedly indicated my preference for a volunteer army, and I think most Canadians will agree with me." He says he has "never heard anyone suggest that the volunteer army is not a desirable thing", and that is perfectly true. On the other hand there are a great many people in this country who think the voluntary system as it is to-day is not fair. There are many people, the legion, members of the opposition, members of the Liberal party, and many others, who have asked for the full operation of the N.R.M.A. for service anywhere in the world. The minister says he thinks most people in Canada agree with him about the volunteer army. That is beside the point. What about the voices of the people in the plebiscite? That certainly called for something different from a volunteer army Those voices called for conscription anywhere in the world, there is no doubt about that, and we have not got it yet.
Just what is wrong with conscription? What is wrong with that method of getting men? The way it is looked on to-day and talked about by ministers suggests a slur on many of those fellows who are drafted, and it is not fair to them. Too much slur is cast on them. Whether you like it or not, to-day you have coercion for volunteering, and why should that slur be cast on those fellows? What is wrong with conscription in the United States or in Great Britain? There is nothing much wrong with it.
What is wrong with the volunteers in Canada?

Members of the
army in Canada in the last year or so had to go around the place wasting their time in making speeches urging on draftees the necessity for volunteering because they could not be taken overseas otherwise. That principle is wrong. Why do they talk so much about the volunteer army and not about having conscription? As I see it, from now on there will not be a volunteer army, because we know

War Appropriation-Labour

very well that we cannot get men without calling them up first and forcing them to enlist, and to my mind it is simply a whim of this government, who are so spineless that they will not put into force the N.R.M.A. to the full extent.
The hon. member for Temiscouata a few minutes ago talked about the unity of Canada, but he said, unity with the Tory party, never. As far as I see it, this whole question of the N.R.M.A. is not a question of the unity of Canada, if the provisions of that act are to be enforced; it is a question of the unity of the Liberal party in this country. This brings me to another point which was suggested to my mind by the hon. member for Nanaimo. We have in Canada to-day some 60,000 men under the N.R.M.A., and of these in the active army, not liable without further government action to service overseas, 34,950. Some of our men in the active army overseas have been there for a long time, men like the hon., member who spoke a little while ago, and yet we have here 34,950 in Canada in the active army who cannot be sent overseas at the present time. The men overseas have been there for four or five years. Could these men here not be sent over to replace those fellows who have been there for four or five years, so as to give them a few weeks' furlough in Canada? Could we not have some proper system of leave whereby those fellows could have a chance to get back?
As the hon. member for Nanaimo said, one of the worst things facing the* troops overseas is homesickness. The United States have made an arrangement for leave for their men coming from the front from different quarters. They have been only three and a half years in the war and we have been in from the beginning. It does not seem fair to have these men over here and the others overseas for so long.

If I might rise to a point of order, I have been on deck for nearly three days now and we have not got the first item through. I have no objection to sitting here until the resurrection, but I think most of the hon. members have. I have no objection to answering questions that affect my department particularly, but I object to wandering all over the lot. The hon. member for St. Paul's is wandering off into the Department of National Defence. I do wish that the hon. member would stay within my department, so that we may at least. get some of the other departments that have to do with the war appropriation bill before the committee in the not very distant future.

The CHAIRMAN; The point of order is well taken in connection with the questions that have been brought up by the hon. member for St. Paul's. I gave readily-I was going to say joyfully-a certain amount of latitude to the hon. member for Greenwood and the hon. member for Nanaimo because it was the first time they had spoken in the committee for years. I believe the time has now arrived when we should get down to the item that is before the committee and stay with it, if possible. I think we should undertake to avoid the multiple repetitions that we have had since the beginning of the discussion. I sincerely appeal to the hon. members of the committee.

I bow to your ruling. I would not have spoken in this way were it not for the fact that this matter is uppermost in my mind, and' in the second place I listened to the hon. member for Temiscouata talking about everything in the world outside of this particular item. I know you, Mr. Chairman, are fair in these things, but I think if you had held the hon. member for Temiscouata a little closer to the subject it might have been a great deal better for everybody.
My speech has been interrupted by a point of order. I have only a few more words to say. As far as this is concerned, I like to see fairness in these things, and if the hon. member for Temiscouata is going to occupy the time of this committee by wandering all over the place, as he did to-night, then I think he should be called to order immediately.
The only other thing I have to say is that in all fairness to the men overseas-
Order.
I have said I have a few remarks to make-

I say in all justice to these men overseas-and I mean it-we should do something about it, if possible. Instead of having these fellows who are sitting back here in the forces in Canada doing nothing, it seems to me that the government might put into full force the N.R.M.A. and send them overseas and let the men overseas have a chance to come back.

I have one or two questions I should like to ask before the item carries. First of all I do not think we have had a break-down of the sum of something over $11,000,000 submitted to us. I find from previous reports that these figures can be

War Appropriation-Labour
broken into (a) the various sections of the department such as the office of the director, headquarters in Ottawa, administration; (b) mobilization division; (c) the man-power records, and (d) the amount set aside to be spent by the unemployment insurance commission for work performed on behalf of national selective service. I should like the minister to explain the difference between the figure as set out on page 396 of Hansard of February 11, which shows that the appropriation for the year 1943-44 was $8,680,225, whereas this amount is $9,845,948. Would the minister be good enough to explain that? Then I have one or two other simple ones that I should like to ask.

I will give my hon. friend the breakdown of the $11,000,000 odd. It is as follows:	Labour supply, $811,879.
There is a decrease of $4,496 there. Mobilization, $3,250,000. There is an increase of $157,000 there. Unemployment insurance commission $6,275,150. There is an increase of $900,000 there. The minister has not explained the reason for the difference between the figure set out on page 413 of Hansard and the figure of $9,845,948.37 on the sheet which has been supplied to us.

In the morning edition of the Ottawa Citizen of a few days ago there appeared certain advertisements, presumably from the national selective department. J should like to draw this one particularly to the attention of the minister. It reads as follows:
Special representative wanted. A leading life insurance company requires special representative in Cornwall and district. He must be a man of character and ambition, a real worker, age thirty ' to fifty. The position offers an attractive life career, with opportunities for advancement. Other benefits include sickness and pension provisions. Previous experience not necessary. The right applicant will ibe given a special training course to fit him for his responsibilities. Apply in writing, selective service, F.M. 374.
What are the circumstances surrounding such advertising, and why does national selective service go to the expense of advertising for a leading life insurance company that could well afford to pay for its own advertising?

Of course, one cannot advertise in this country except for very few 100-162J
categories, namely, household help and things like that. What is done is, we route all these people through selective service so that we know where everybody is and have the measure of control that we have. That particular company would pay for the advertising. The individual would be routed through our office, and then of course we would have some say whether the individual could go into life insurance or whether he should not be in some other priority.

Under national selective service in the west, if a man is called up to take his medical and makes application for
War Appropriation-Labour

exemption on the ground that he is a conscientious objector, his case is left entirely to an alternative service officer appointed under order in council. In most cases single men who make application on these grounds are asked, I think quite justly, to take service in some other effective work in Canada. If they are put into agriculture they are asked to take employment under contract, under which they are paid the going wage, which I believe is $40 a month. One of these men is allowed $25 for his own expenses and is asked to pay the balance of $15 to the Red Cross, which I think is quite justifiable. Recently, however, my attention was drawn to the case of a man married in 1937, with a wife and two children, living on a quarter-section of land. He did not make application for exemption on the ground that he was essential to agriculture; he claimed exemption because he was of the Doukhobor faith, and acting in good faith he made application on these grounds. His contract calls for him to employ himself at the rate of $40 a month. Of this total he is allowed $25 for himself, and apparently for his wife and two children, and he is required to pay the balance of $15 to the Red Cross. This man claims he is unable to carry out these instructions, and he wrote asking if this was considered fair treatment. I should like to know whether there is any method by which this man could obtain redress from the alternative service officer with respect to his dependents.

I think the channel is there. My hon. friend has stated the facts, but this man can appeal to the associate director, who is in charge of that phase of my organization.
Mr. CASTLEDEN; The alternative service officer?

Yes, the director in
Ottawa.
He can apply to the director in Ottawa?

Yes.
Mr. CASTLEDEN; Who is that director in Ottawa?
Mr. Westman. If my hon. friend will send the application to me I will see that it gets to the right man.

I wrote the minister about this case. It seemed to me that in spite of the minister's letter to the effect that the alternative service officer has a staff to investigate these cases, in this instance some-

thing was done which had not been properly investigated, and I was wondering whether there were many other similar cases.
No.

I should like the minister to deal with the point I raised yesterday in regard to the young men who have been given postponements because they are working on farms, and who are being called to the district depots for reexamination. Yesterday I asked the minister if there was to be any change in the procedure, and I wonder if he could give an answer to-night.

We have to know where people are. We may give a man a postponement because he is essential to agriculture, but if we are not careful he may pop up in some industry in Toronto or Montreal or Quebec or some other city. We have to keep our fingers on everyone, at least to know where they are; so that I cannot give my hon. friend the assurance that there will be any change in that policy in the immediate future.

Am I to take it from the remarks of the minister that any young man now working on a farm who has a postponement will be granted a further extension after May 1 or June 1, when his postponement expires?
Absolutely.
Does it make any difference whether that man continues to work for someone else or if he starts out on his own?
As long as he is engaged in agriculture; that is the essential point.

I was in the gallery when the hon. member for St. Paul's spoke. I wondered if my memory was good, so I looked in the "Parliamentary Guide" and confirmed my recollection that he had graduated from the military college at Kingston. When I see him looking as imposing as usual I think he must be a major-general, but I am surprised that a man educate'd at the military college at Kingston should be so strong for conscription though he did not himself volunteer during the last war; and I make that statement as a civilian.

I agree with your ruling, Mr. Chairman, and I shall speak of a more interesting matter. The question now before the committee is undoubtedly one of the most important we shall have to discuss during this war, namely, the question of selective service. I regret very much that some facts have not been recorded by the registrar's office, or by national defence headquarters in each military district. For instance, I asked the following two questions, which may be condensed into one:
1.	Since 1940, how many requests for leave or postponement of training have been submitted, by the army to the mobilization board of each of the military districts other than the military district of Quebec for soldiers or conscripts who were farmers, farmers' sons or farm helpers?
2.	In how many of such cases did the said boards (a) recommend leave; (to) refuse to recommend leave?
Here are the answers that were given to-day:
1 and 2. The army does not maintain records on the number of applications for leave referred to mobilization boards nor on the number of those recommended or not recommended by such boards. To ascertain this information it would be necessary to examine the personal file in the district records office of every soldier.
Application for postponement of training is made direct to mobilization boards toy the individual concerned before his enrolment into the army.
The matter is of great importance, and I know that since the thing has not been done before it would take some time now to gather the information. But there was no excuse for the registrar, and there was no excuse for the headquarters in each district not gathering that information, because each case was submitted by the army to the mobilization board. It is within my knowledge that in very deserving applications for leave the rulings of the mobilization board supported the contention of the army. Very seldom did the men get justice before mobilization boards, when their cases were submitted to those boards by the army.
I see some hon. members opposite who have spoken loudly of their love for the farmer. There is a small number of members of parliament who have done something for the farmer by succeeding in having national war service regulations and mobilization regulations amended. I, for one, have done my share in that work, because I know very well the usefulness of the farmer on the farm. It is a great mistake to tell farmers that their first duty is not that of cultivating the farm, but that it is to enlist in the armed forces. Where would the army be if it had no food? Some country-wide re-forms were gained for the
farmer by the small group of members who were fighting for him last year, and whose claims are on record in the Votes and Proceedings of this chamber. They have got something for the farmer. They have tried to secure recognition of the importance of his work on the farm.
For instance, the former chairman of the Quebec mobilization board had the feeling that all those ?f military age who did not join the army were slackers, and unworthy of British citizenship. He once wrote me:
You must understand that we cannot postpone the farmers' service indefinitely.
In his view, a postponement was a favour, not a right in virtue of the law. He and his brother colleagues of the board did not understand either the letter or the spirit of the regulations, and we have had to put up a struggle for the farmers; for everyone will realize the loss that must result when the farmers are taken away from their farms. It is disastrous.
I had the unpleasant duty of reporting him to his minister, who entirely agreed with me, to the effect that the farmers had the same rights as others occupied in seasonal and essential industries, and were entitled to postponement. The staff of the board had to be changed because of their refractory turn of mind.
Now, when we hear some people saying that the farmers are exempted from service, it is untrue because there are a good many farmers who went to their training in good faith but they were kept in the army by men who are not expert in agriculture. There are many farms that cannot produce as much now as they did before, and that is exactly the reason.
The first reform was to secure postponements of six months instead of four for all those engaged in an essential industry. The second reform was that instructions were given to all the national war services boards in accordance with the statement made in the house on November 11, 1941, by the then minister now Mr. Justice Thorson. These were his words:
Mr. Thorson: My answer will be in reply to the question asked by the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) and the hon. member for Hastings-Peterborough (Mr. White). No postponement can be for longer than six months, but when that six months period is over, another^ postponement may be granted. The jurisdiction of the board is not confined to the second postponement; the board may grant one or more extensions of the original postponement, but each postponement must be for a period of not longer than six months. In each case the board looks at the application
War Appropriation-Labour

from the point of view of the national interest and deals with each ease upon its merits. It has complete jurisdiction in granting or refusing an application for a postponement order.
The ex-chairman was a judge, and he had had the distinction of having four of his judgments reversed at one term of the court of appeal. Under his chairmanship the jurisprudence of the board was that all farmers who worked as lumberjacks during the winter were not bona fide farmers. He always refused a postponement in such cases.
I succeeded at last in having him remove that from the picture, but he was responsible to a large extent for the otherwise inexcusable farm and labour shortage in the Quebec district. The representative of the farmers was a former wood-scaler of the Power Lumber company of St-. Pacome. Both the cx-chair-man and he were the choice of the Minister of National Defence for Air. Originally the third member of the board was a former mayor of Quebec city, and the father-in-law of the D.M.O. of military district No. 5. He died and was replaced by a labour leader who was so silly that I had only to mention in the house a long distance telephone conversation I had with him to have him replaced by another man whom I do not know, and whom I have not yet called over the telephone.
It was quite a feat to get rid of those people whom Ottawa seemed to consider more indispensable on the board than the farmers on the land, the lumberjacks in the forests, the firemen and the brakemen on the trains, and so on. And there have been advertisements appearing in the press with pictures of the Minister of Labour. I had so much trouble with the board in Quebec city that I had to write them to the effect that if they did not consider seriously the cases of some farmers' sons who were working in the forests during the lumbering season, I would have to write to the papers and ask them if they were really authorized to publish the minister's picture, or if it was just an April fool joke. The picture of the minister was put alongside the statement that those who were working in the forests would be considered as working in an essential industry. It is not surprising that these things happen when we consider the point of view of the imperialists, those who are blind and who do not realize the importance of having men in all the various fields of endeavour.
I complained about the office of the Quebec registrar. There have been son*e changes, but the clean-up has not gone far enough. I commend the minister for having put out one of the assistant registrars. I complained about him three years ago and it has taken that long to get rid of him. What did he do
FMr. Pouliot.]
while he was there? What did the incompetent judge do while he was chairman? Many applicants suffered injustices and many farmers have been placed in the position of producing much less because of the stupidity of these men. I want the minister to understand that I have no grievance against anyone. When I complain about some one on these boards I do so because I know there is inefficiency. I try to help him by giving him information which he could not secure otherwise. Many people are afraid to tell the truth because they fear they will be penalized. They fear that rulings will be given by these men if they denounce them to the minister. It is not a question of carrying tales, to use the popular expression; it is a question of informing the minister of what is going on.
The proper way to secure the right information as to how the law is being administered is not to write to the guilty parties for a report. I know this man is incompetent because I know this is not the only occasion mistakes have been made. What happened? Most of the time he was asked to report on my complaint and it is not surprising that his answer was his own justification. Things got so bad that two years ago I had to assign as a witness the very man who had been fired by the minister after three years of complaints. An investigation was carried on in court before a district magistrate. I asked the selective service to secure a copy of the reporter's notes, but I do not think this has been done. I gave my services free and I did not feel like paying to have the stenographer's notes transcribed for the government. I expected the department to do that. I do not know if it has been done yet, but many months after the case was over, the notes had not been transcribed by the court stenographer. This inquiry showed the incompetency and inefficiency of that man who had the power of life or death on draftees.
I read what was said yesterday and I have listened to what has been said to-day about military district No. 5. A clean-up is needed in the army headquarters and national selective service in Quebec city. I should like to say a word of praise for the representative of selective service on the mobilization board in that city. The hon. member for Quebec West and South (Mr. Parent) says that I am right in complaining about the army in military district No. 5. French Canadians are getting a raw deal from French Canadian officers who have never been at war. I do not say that it is only French Canadians who are treating my compatriots in the province of Quebec in that way because at headquarters in Quebec city there are people from

War Appropriation-Labour
all over the country. But French Canadians are not getting a fair deal from the medical corps of the army. I think I have given enough instances of the trouble they have.
Mr. Chairman, you ruled that this debate should be confined to the Department of Labour. We are now getting into a discussion of army matters.

My answer is quite
obvious. The minister gave figures which had been provided by the army. All day yesterday this was the subject matter of the debate, which resumed at five-fifteen this afternoon until six o'clock, and then from eight o'clock until the present time. I complained that the minister was not the boss of his own department, that he had to rely upon figures over which he had no control. I am ready to help him to the limit, although I do not know what the limit is. Even though we are at war we should have reforms at and from general headquarters.
As my hon. friend knows, these farmers are called up for medical examinations. They receive these notices from the registrar who is under the minister. Then the mobilization boards which are under the Minister of Labour decide upon matters submitted to them by the Department of National Defence. How is it possible to discuss the operation of this law under the Department of Labour without mentioning what happens in the Department of National Defence? It is all the one and the same thing. It is not a question of being prejudiced; it is a question of seeing that Canadian people do their best in producing war materials on the farm, in industry and everywhere else. There has been a complete ignoring of the importance of the work being carried on by men in essential industry.
At this point I should like to ask the minister a most important question. What is the arrangement between his department and Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway company regarding the calling up of men to the camps? There is one man in the C.N.R. and another in the C.P.R. who have the power of life and death over railway men. These men are located in Montreal and they decide whether a man is essential in his own district. To my own knowledge men have been recommended by their own divisional superintendents and this recommendation has been reversed by these men who are in Montreal. It is Mr. Edge in the C.N.R., and there is another man in the C.P.R. If a man does not have a recommendation from either of these gentlemen he goes automatically to the camp, no matter how essential he may be as a railway man.
There are essential positions in the railway business. Is an old man who is past the superannuation age, who can be seen at the same hour every day at the news-stand in the Chateau Laurier, to decide whether a man is essential? That old man has outlived his usefulness and yet he has the power of life and death over other railway men. As I say, he is located in Ottawa and the other two are located in Montreal. These men have the power of sending to the training camps men who have had long experience in railway work.

My hon. friend is stating that these men must have a recommendation from either the Canadian Pacific Railway company or the Canadian National Railways that they are essential. I thought, Mr. Chairman, we were discussing the labour question and not men for the army. No doubt the minister has had difficulties in choosing these men, but I am pretty sure that he would not have chosen them unless he had had recommendations from the essential war industries, like the CP.R. and the C.N.R.; and if he receives the recommendation that somebody should be taken on, even though he is over-age, it is reasonable to assume that under present conditions the Minister of Labour and the selective service board will accept the recommendations of those who say that certain men are essential to -their operations. I think we are going beyond our scope when we try to discuss military matters under this item.
In reply to the hon. member for Skeena, who will not be a member after the next election-
Thank you. Mr. Chairman, I have just as good a chance, I think, if I decide to stand, as the hon. member for Temiscouata.
We can decide that between ourselves.
Order.

Here we are discussing, precisely, national selective service, and I have been speaking in the first place of a man who was an appointee of the Department of Labour. I wonder why I should not have the right to discuss the case of a man who was not appointed by the C.P.R. or the C.N.R., but by the Minister of Labour himself. That is the first point. In the second place I mentioned the name of one of the other men merely at the request of one of my colleague#, and I have said nothing uncivil in that respect. I complain of the fact. I do not complain of these two men; I complain of the fact that they are given the power of life and death over railway men who are essentia! to the war effort but who cannot resume their activities
War Appropriation-Labour

as railway men because Mr. So-and-so does not want to recommend them on account of an arrangement which has been made between the Department of Labour and the railway. If this condition does not affect the hon. member in his constituency of Skeena, because he has not a large number of railway men in his riding, it may affect the transportation of his constituents or of their goods. We need good men, men of experience, to carry on their work as railway men, and it is because I realize the great importance of the railway business that I am asking some questions of the minister. I would tell the hon. member for Skeena that I was in the house a long time before he arrived, and I have been-

I have been here for fifteen years; and as far as the constituency of Skeena is concerned, just about one-third of the population is either dependent in the matter of transportation on the railway or on coastal shipping.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: If I may be allowed to refer to the point of order raised by the hon. member for Victoria, Ontario, surely after three full days of discussion we should come down at some time to work on the definite item before the committee. I appeal to all hon. members to realize that, with all the speeches which we have had for the past two days and more, this item is not yet passed. The Chair must take some responsibility and insist that speeches must be relevant to the matter before the committee. Surely, after nearly three days' discussion, so much repetition is unnecessary. Much of the discussion is out of order.

I regret that I have to repeat things, but it is at the request of the hon. member for Skeena. This matter has not been brought before the house during this session, and it is the time to ask for some information from the Minister of Labour about the arrangement that has been made between his department and the railway companies. I have been told that there is an arrangement whereby those who have had one month's training go automatically to the army as soon as their leave has expired and that further postponement is granted to those who have never done any training. I would ask the minister to be kind enough to give us full information about the arrangement which has been made between his department and the railway companies regarding the status of men of military age who have railway experience.

Mr. Chairman, it is
simple. It is an arrangement which exists in every big corporation in this country, and it

is that the personnel managers of these particular railroads-I think Mr. Edge is one of them and Mr. Brydon-Jack is the other-are responsible for any recommendations made to the mobilization board with respect to the postponement of men engaged in these companies. That is the general procedure. A man applies for postponement; it is either supported or not supported by the employer. These two gentlemen happen to be the chiefs of personnel of these two great railroads. In some other organization it would be someone else. It is just as simple as that. There is no secret about it. They speak for the company.
Mr. Chairman-
