speechtext: Order.
If my hon. friend permits me a minute, I will ask the minister if he will be kind enough to table the correspondence between the railways and the Department of Labour regarding this matter.
I shall be glad to do that. Anything for peace and quietness.
May I ask the minister whether the national resources mobilization board is supreme in each military district, or whether there is any authority or board above it to which an appeal may be directed?
The board is supreme. There is no appeal.

Mr. Chairman. I feel it is my duty to say a few words on these estimates, although I am anxious that the debate be concluded with all possible speed. But first, I may be allowed to heartily congratulate the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Chambers) for the splendid speech he delivered to-night. His stand proves that his patriotism is not of the parlour variety but of the staunchest kind; it is the brand of patriotism professed by those who love their country as we do, and who are willing to risk their lives for the defence of the endangered fatherland. In my own name and on behalf of all those who feel as I do, I wish to congratulate him from the bottom of my heart, on his stand and his sentiments.
We have entered this war because we really thought that the country was in danger. The great majority of the hon. members of this house, in 1939, supported the government when they declared war on Germany. If the elementary principles of philosophy I learned in my student days have any value and one of which is that common sense is a test of truth, I believe that the great majority of the members of this house, having sup-

War Appropriation-Labour
ported the action taken by the government when they declared war, we must have been right. We realized that our country was in danger. We have felt that it was worth risking all that we hold as most valuable to defend what our fatherland, Canada, means to us. As for me, Mr. Chairman, such were my feelings and such they have remained. After France, like other European nations, was overrun in June, 1940, I felt that if Great Britain had been crushed at a time when, following the Dunkirk evacuation, neither Canada, England nor the United States were prepared to meet the onslaught, this would have been the end of our liberties, of everything worthwhile in Canada. Therefore, since every patriotic citizen who really loves his country must be anxious to defend it at the risk of his life, and since every worthy citizen is naturally patriotic, we must realize that the youth who have voluntarily enlisted for overseas service or are still willing to do so when circumstances permit, deserve our admiration and are worthy of the pride we feel for them. Those who do not enlist, even though they would be most anxious to do so, have been prevented from taking that course by the selective service. In a great majority of cases, young men brought up on farms have been prevented from enlisting because it is as if each of them had been told: "Young man, in spite of your desire to fight for your country overseas, it is our duty to prevent you from going there because we want you to produce foodstuffs for those who are going to fight over there." Therefore, a great majority of farmers' sons have been, as it were, frozen on the land. The same thing may be said about those who are called upon to work in war industries. If what I say is true, I submit that farmers' sons have not enlisted in larger numbers because they could not do so or because it was thought that their immediate duty lay in the production of foodstuffs for our soldiers and the armies of our allies. My hon. friend the member for Beauharnois-Laprairie (Mr. Raymond) told us last night how terrible it is for a farmer to inform against his son. However, I do not know any bona fide farmers in my constituency, or elsewhere whose sons have been refused a postponement. Therefore, as I know very well the hon. member for Beauharnois-Laprairie, I was rather puzzled by the statement he made last night about farmers' sons. He knows as well as I do that not one bona fide farmer's son has been called up and that, if he has been called he was granted a postponement. Therefore, the father has not been forced to inform against his son since it is the duty of both the father and the son to produce more and more.
There is another matter broached by the hon. member for Beauharnois-Laprairie about which I would like to offer some explanation, not with the intention of lecturing him, but at least so that the citizens of our province may know that if a member protested against that order in council while all others kept silent, it was not because anyone wanted to admit the accuracy of the statement made by the hon. member for Beauharnois-Laprairie, and which had reference to the order in council he mentioned last night as reported on page 2534 of Hansard. He said that the government had been unfair to Canadians of French extraction when they passed order in council No. 1355, dated March 4, 1944, which contains the following provision:
The minister, upon being informed by the Department of National Defence that a specified number of men are required for military training, may instruct any registrar to apply these regulations to a specified number of men from iris division, and may inform a registrar how many French-speaking men are required.
And the hon. member for Beauharnois-Laprairie said:
I ask the minister why he has inserted in this order in council a special provision relating to French-speaking Canadians. I thought that in this country of ours we were all Canadians and that when men are called into the army there should be no distinction between French Canadians or English Canadians or Canadians of any other race, because we are all Canadians. I fail to see the abject of this special distinction applying to French Canadians.
Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to answer on behalf of the minister. The hon. minister can well take care of himself. If I bring the matter up, it is only to state humbly that the hon. member for Chambly-Rouville differs from the hon. member for Beauharnois-Laprairie in his interpretation of the order.
Hear, hear.

My hon. friend knows perfectly well, or at least should know, that in the very first year of the war, in 1940, when the National War Services Department was set up, the hon. Minister of National War Services and the other ministers of the crown decided in their wisdom-and we congratulate them for it-that English-speaking Canadians would receive their military training in the English language, and that the French-speaking Canadians would get theirs in their own language. And then, as officers were not in sufficient number-the hon. member for Portneuf (Mr. Gauthier), a former officer himself, knows it very well-officers' training schools were set up throughout Canada and particularly in the province of Quebec. Thus a great many officers were trained and formed, so that, since the

War Appropriation-Labour

beginning of the war, any young Frenchspeaking Canadian, whether he enlists voluntarily or is called up for home defence in Canada or in Canada's territorial waters, is directed to a training centre where he is instructed in French by French-Canadian officers. The hon. member for Beauharaois-Laprairie must be aware of that. Since 1940 every member in the house and every army training centre have received a pamphlet, "The National War Services Regulations, 1940" (Consolidation 1941). And if the hon. member for Portneuf who is presently, I suppose, the representative of the party headed by the hon. member for Beauharnois-Laprairie, cares to look up page 7, paragraph 9, of that pamphlet, he will note that this same paragraph of the order in council exists since the beginning of the war. I shall not quote the whole paragraph, but merely the part which deals with French-Canadian recruits. Subsection 2 of section 9 reads as follows:
The minister shall inform each divisional registrar concerned of the number of Frenchspeaking men who are required to report for military training to an indicated place or places and at an indicated time.
Since then, and precisely on account of this section, these instructions are followed by National Defence and mobilization officials. When the number of French-Canadian recruits who report for military training is known, they are immediately sent to training schools staffed by French-Canadian officers who teach them in their own tongue. More than that, they are supplied with French textbooks. So that when my hon. friend from Beauharnois-Laprairie attempted to take the hon. Minister of Labour to task for this section of the order in council which he quoted last evening, he afforded the other hon. members of this house who are of French descent the opportunity to look up the National War Services regulations and to tell our hon. friends, the members of the Bloc Populaire, that the purpose, the motive, the reason why this clause was inserted,-and is still in the regulations-was exactly to give fair play to Canadians of French descent who wish to do their duty and defend their country.
(Text) Mr. GILLIS: I am just as anxious as the minister to see the item pass, but this is about the only chance we have to get information on certain matters about which we receive inquiries. I wish to try to get some information from the minister on the unemployment situation, and I rise for that purpose. So many complicated statements are made that I am beginning to wonder whether anyone knows exactly what the employment requirements of the country are. Since the minister has presented his estimates he has stated

that he could use 160,000 people if he could find them. Notwithstanding that statement one finds statements in the press and statements emanating from national selective service that would lead one to believe that either those in selective service who are directly responsible for the problem have very little knowledge of it or the minister is out in his estimates. It is to clarify that, in my own mind at least, that I want to get some information. For example, on March 23 the Ottawa Citizen carried the following statement :
Mr. Redvers Pratt, local manager of the office of employment and selective service, said to-day he called on contractors unaware of the surplus of workmen to begin operations immediately.
That is, in the building trade, and he goes on to point out that he has listed in his office some 121 carpenters out of work, also a great number of bricklayers, lathers, painters and a considerable number of heavy labourers and so forth. That is right here in Ottawa from one of the main offices. You find the union of carpenters, bricklayers, painters and labourers in Toronto writing in and protesting against the fact that employees in the building trades, old men who were unfit for, or not eligible for military service are being replaced by ablebodied Royal Canadian Air Force personnel. They are taking over the regular employment of those men who must earn their own living in that way. I am not going to elaborate on that. It has many ramifications. There is waste in several directions there. I am absolutely convinced of the trustworthiness of the sources of the information. It has been a matter of controversy for some time between the Department of Labour and the unions concerned.
I hold in my hand correspondence of as recent a date as April 18. The fact of the matter is the R.C.A.F. personnel are replacing civilian personnel in that trade. More serious than that is a circular letter issued by the office of the manager of selective service at Dawson Creek, British Columbia. According to this letter it would appear that there has been some change in the rates of pay of employees employed on the Alaska highway. A new schedule was posted which in effect changed from an hourly basis to a monthly basis most of the employees employed on that project in a maintenance capacity. This change is looked upon by the employees as a reduction in wages of approximately S125 a month.
That is a substantial reduction in the change-over. Coinciding with the posting of the new schedule we find the manager of employment and selective service in that area

War Appropriation-Labour
issuing a notice which is certainly not in line with the statement made by the minister on the matter of employment. I shall quote a couple of paragraphs of it, because if the minister is not aware of it he should be. The notice reads as follows:
To: All Canadian employees employed by United States engineers department.
I regret very much that due to pressure of business I am unable to call upon each and every camp individually and give a talk regarding the proposed set-up for Canadian employees on the maintenance of highway flight strips and airports and the conditions pertaining thereto.
However, Mr. McDonald of the labour relations, U.S. government, who is a Canadian, has kindly consented to give a talk on such conditions which have been posted in each and every camp.
I want the minister to take notice of this statement:
There is one thing I would like to impress upon you. As no doubt some of you are aware, conditions outside at the present time are not of the very best meaning by this there has been heavy lay-offs of workers throughout Canada as a whole and in many centres where there has been war projects of various descriptions the wages have lapsed back to those that were paid prior to the war.
It is the intention of both United States and Canadian governments at the present time to retain in the neighbourhood of five to six hundred individuals for the fore-mentioned maintenance work.
There is no indication at the present time of any new projects being opened up in Canada with the result there will be a difficult matter to absorb in Canadian industry the hundreds that are now idle throughout the prairie provinces alone and I would suggest and advise that those of you who are desirous of having employment for the duration of the war plus six months thereafter at a still fair wage schedule as quoted by Mr. McDonald, would consider very seriously of making their intentions known immediately to their superior official.
I cannot understand a letter like that going out from a national selective service office. I do not imagine the central office in Ottawa would have any knowledge of it, nor that it would have their sanction, because that officer is giving a wrong picture of the employment situation, if the minister is correct, and is using his office to coerce the men concerned into accepting a very substantial reduction in wages. In the light of press statements emanating to a large extent from selective service officials, and the minister's statement that he could find employment for some 160,000 people if he had them, I should like him to tell the committee briefly just where this employment is available, because in the province from which I come a large number of men are unemployed. I receive letters from them from time to time, and I should like to be able to advise them where they might find employment. I am not going to 100-1631
take up any more time on this subject; one might speak on it for hours, but I should like the minister to make a brief statement indicating the sections of Canada where there is a shortage of labour, and of course I should like him to make some comments on this letter. What I am principally concerned about, of course, is to discover where in Canada there is a shortage of labour in any given industry, so that when we receive inquiries we may be able to advise people accordingly. Certainly, men are not needed in the building industry.

They are needed in
every packing plant in Canada.

That is good. Then, as a
matter of labour relations, I should like the minister to tell me whether it is the policy of his department under selective service to permit regular members of the building trades, mechanics and so on, to be replaced by service personnel and thrown on to unemployment insurance. This is an old difficulty which, to my knowledge, has been encountered for the last eighteen months; it has been a matter of controversy between selective service and the service departments, and I think the time has come when the Department of Labour should decide exactly what is to be done, since it is the prerogative of this department to look after such matters.

I was speaking in round figures the other day when I mentioned the 160,000 people who were needed. In the A, B. and C priority industries there is at the present time a shortage of 103.659 males. There are vacancies for 15,709 loggers and for 51,475 females in all occupations. This is the latest return.

Could the minister give us
any idea of the sections of Canada where these people are needed?

I am trying to get that break-down now. In regard to the letter read by my hon. friend I can only say that in a large organization such as we are administering, letters like this do go out sometimes. As soon as we had knowledge of this letter it was suppressed; that is as far as I can go in that direction. In regard to people being unemployed, the hon. gentleman knows as well as I do that there will be pockets of unemployment. That is inevitable in a country with seasonal employment like Canada; for short periods, at any rate, there will be unemployment, particularly in the building trades, let us say. The men engaged in those trades understand it; in fact the wage structure is predicated upon that fact. I am not going into the history of the development of the wage structure in the building industry or any
War Appropriation-Labour

other industry, but that fact is understood. In regard to the information requested by the hon. gentleman as to where labour shortages exist, as I said in connection with another matter naturally we who are engaged in the central control deal in the large numbers while the local offices deal with matters in the field. I shall endeavour to give my hon. friend the figures he desires; they are available any time he wants them. I can send them over to him, unless he would like them on the record.
I believe they should be on the record.
Very well, but my hon. friend can see what I am up against.
It is not necessary to read them.
This is a pretty big proposition.
Table them.

I shall be glad to do that, but I do not think they should go into Hansard; they would cover several pages. My hon. friend wants an indication of where there are vacancies, I suppose particularly in his own province.
Yes.

I shall be glad to give my hon. friend these figures. With reference to competition in the services, particularly in the building trades, that is an old story, and it is pretty hard to draw the line between where the functions of the armed services end and where the work of the building trades begins. I was not aware that we were having any serious difficulty at the present time, I mean in a large way. That condition might exist somewhere temporarily, but I know we maintain liaison with the service departments, and any protests or complaints or representations are taken up with the other departments expeditiously. I think that is as far as I can go. I know of no specific instances at the moment of complaints of competition between men in the services and those engaged in ordinary, everyday labour.

I have in my hand a list sent me by the national union of carpenters and bricklayers of Toronto. The complaint is that at No. 1 equipment depot twelve civilian carpenters have been laid off and replaced by R.C.A.F. personnel. The matter is now being adjudicated, I understand, by two or three different departments.

That is in the day to Jay administration of the department; there is nothing new about that.
[Mr. Mitchell. 1

You take a boy into the air force, and the country goes to great expense in order to train him. Then when you have him trained, when he might be able to make a real contribution from a military point of -view, you make use of that boy to replace a civilian carpenter, who is forced back upon unemployment insurance. I cannot see the sense of it.

I would ask the minister to answer a question I had placed on the order paper, giving the figures as to the number of persons, both male and female, registered as unemployed, and the number of persons placed by the unemployment service. The figure came up to January 27. Would the minister bring it up to the end of April?
The hon. member wants the figure for unemployment insurance?
No; the number registered at employment offices as seeking employment. If I remember correctly, on January 27, the figure was 67,000.
I shall be glad to have that information to-morrow.

Mr. Chairman, I was listening a little while ago to the hon. member for Chambly-Rouville (Mr. Dupuis) who, outside as well as within this chamber has become a most powerful champion of an all-out war effort in the province of Quebec. I rise at this moment not for the purpose of answering his speech but rather in an attempt to put things in their proper light. Since he spoke of the declaration of war, and though he was out of order, I shall take the liberty of following in his steps so as to straighten the facts.
His speech would lead us to believe that most of the members of the house have voted in favour of participation in this war, though ne did not expressly say so. His remarks might give the impression that the members actually voted on this question, while no vote was taken on the declaration of war. If the hon. member wishes to refer to Hansard of that year, he will note that the declaration of war was agreed to on division, following an observation made by the then leader of the C.C.F. party, Mr. Woodsworth, who said that several members opposed the motion. The speaker having said: "Carried", an hon. member added: "On division." That is how the declaration of war was agreed to. Two days later, we were called upon to vote on the question of participation, that is on a motion of the Minister of Finance asking for an appropriation of 8100,000,000. Sixteen members voted against participation, and the hon. member for Chambly-Rouville was not one of them.

War Appropriation-Labour

I am proud
of the fact that I was not one of them.

The hon. member for Chambly-Rouville has talked about farmers' sons. He has made an effort once more. Last year the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot)-I would not compare him with the hon. member for Chambly-Rouville when it comes to helping farmers' sons, as that would not be a mark of favour or of praise-made a motion to get exemptions for farmers' sons. I wonder if the hon. member for Chambly-Rouville voted for that motion.
(Translation): The government had already decided that farmers' sons were exempted.
Certainly, and Le Canada and Le Soleil published headlines six inches high that read: "Farmers' Sons Are Exempted". Since when are they exempted?
They still are.

They are not. They get a postponement, and they have to lose hours and days of.work every time it must be renewed. If the hon, member thinks that is right, I do not.
And when the hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Roy) last year moved an amendment to the address dealing with farmers' sons, and when we of the Bloc Populaire presented an amendment to the amendment in which we asked that farmers' sons be exempted, the hon. member voted against it. He had once made an effort that had been too much for him, he did not try to repeat it.
The hon. member finds that the member for Beauharnois-Laprairie (Mr. Raymond) goes too far, that he is too critical. But the farmers' sons who have volunteered were certainly not compelled to enlist for overseas service. One of my fellow parishioners who had volunteered has just returned from overseas. But in regard to those who were called for home defence, it frequently happens that farmers' sons had to remain four months and even six months in the army before their release could be secured.
There are not five per cent of these in your constituency.

I repeit that in several cases farmers' sons were compelled to remain a long time in the army ' before obtaining their release.
(Text) Mr. MITCHELL: If I might just interject a word: I think my hon. friend is discussing the position of employees in agriculture, under the national selective service regulations. I think I had better read the
regulations, so that they may be on record. This is the law. It is not an opinion; it is the law, and it says:
the board shall, upon the application of a person employed in agriculture, grant him a postponing order until further notice, until it is established to the satisfaction of the board that such person is not an essential worker in agriculture or that such person has at any time since March 23, 1942, ceased to be a person employed in agriculture; but any postponing order made on such grounds may be cancelled by the board, if it is satisfied that the person has, at any time since March 23, 1942, ceased to be a person employed in agriculture.
So that it is automatic.

I was just telling the hon. member for Chambly-Rouville that we have cases where farmers' sons were called to report to the army, or to pass their medical examinations; and sometimes because they have delayed in filling out their report they have been kept in the army for from four to six months. These were farmers' sons, bona fide farmers' sons, and I can give the cases to the minister, if he wants to have them. That is what I was saying; I was not speaking generally. I was telling the minister that there were cases where farmers' sons were obliged to ask for delay, and when they wanted to obtain that delay they had to use hours and sometimes days to attend before the commission in Quebec, before a decision was given. I think I am right in saying that.
I should like to see the facts in the case before expressing an opinion. That farmer may have had more sons; I do not know.
This is a special case, and I will give the information to the minister. This boy was kept in the army for four months.
One man in the constituency!

Wait a minute; my hon. friend is braver than he was in Stanstead. This is not the only case I have, and I am positive I am not the only member who could give cases to the minister where farmers' sons have been kept in the army for months. That is not an opinion; it is a fact.
They may not be essential; it is a matter of opinion.
When a farmer has only one son, do you say he is not essential?
It may not be a producing farm.
This time it was a producing farm.
That is what you say; the board might not think so.

If the minister does not wish to take my word, all right; I am honest enough and polite enough to take his.
War Appropriation-Labour
Was he late in applying for postponement?

I would be glad to look into the case for my hon. friend.
Mr.,GAUTHIER: There are cases like that where farmers' sons are still in the army and the minister knows about them. There are cases where men did not report right away. I know of one or two cases where the men did not report for a month or two. One man came in himself and the other was brought in by the mounted police. Are these men being kept in the army as a penalty because they did not report right away?
I do not know the case. My hon. friend knows all about it.
A farmer's son was called by selective service to report and-
He fails to do so.
-he fails to do so, as my hon. friend says. But he reports to the army, and I want to know if he is being kept there as a penalty because he delayed reporting.

I have told my hon. friend that I cannot say. I cannot sit in judgment in this House of Comomns on 1,600,000 people; it is a physical impossibility. If my hon. friend will give me the facts and the numbers of the cases I shall be glad to look into them. The other day I parked my car where I should not have parked it. I got a ticket because I had broken the law. It is just as simple as that. These men were ordered to report and they did not; they broke the law.

But I am asking if this man is being kept in the army as a penalty.
Here is another case. Suppose a man is a specialist in agriculture and was working on a poultry farm as an employee before being called up. He had studied for a number of years and when in the army he endeavoured to get a deferment, which was refused.

That is another instance where I would have to get the particulars. My hon. friend cannot turn this House of Commons into a tribunal. I assume that the board is located in Quebec city and that there would be representatives of agriculture to advise that board, as well as the different agencies interested in the man-power problem generally. A judge of one of the courts acts as chairman, the same as in every other part of Canada. I do not know the particulars of these cases. It may be that this man is the only one in Canada who claims he is a specialist. A man may say he is a farmer and be the only man in Canada who thinks so. Because a man says he is a

farmer does not mean a thing until he is proved to be a farmer by these different agencies.

This man was in British Columbia and he had attended agricultural college for two years before taking this position. He asked for a delay which was refused on the ground that he was not related to his employer. A man who has studied for two years must be a specialist.
It often happens that a man will not tell his commanding officer the same story as he tells his family.
He does not need to tell me his story because I know him personally. I know where he has been working and all about him.

There are lots of men who tell their commanding officers an entirely different story from what they tell at home. Many of these men want to stay in the army when the people back home think they should be home.
He does not want to stay in the army. He asked for a delay and they refused it on the ground that he was not related to his employer.

Mr. Chairman, I was in Quebec last night when I read in the newspapers that entirely unfair attacks from a member of this house against Quebec district had again unfortunately been launched. I was glad to find to-night in L'Action Catholique of Quebec, a rejoinder concerning the gratuitous assertion made yesterday in this house by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker). At page 2498 of Hansard of May 1, I read the following:
In Quebec military district, division F, they called up 8-6 per cent of the total population, or, in that period of time, only 8,724 out of some 460,000 men.
I wonder why some members take pleasure in making such exaggerated statements which invariably refer to the province of Quebec. They afterwards circulate such falsehoods in the English language newspapers of this country. To-night, I read in L'Action Catholique of May 2 a statement from the Quebec district registrar, Mr. Pare. Here is what he says:
It is absolutely untrue that, in Quebec district, only 9,000 out of 460,000 "callable" men have been called up, as was alleged by Mr. John B. Diefenbaker, Progressive-Conservative member for Lake Centre. In the first place, in our district, there are but 180,000 "callable" men, not 460,000 as Mr. Diefenbaker has asserted. Moreover, to date, all these men have been called up and have complied with the law. A certain number have been sent to military camps, others have been found physi-

cally unfit, while a third group, after having complied with the law, have been granted postponements under the regulations exempting from military service farmers' sons, lumbermen, fishermen and persons employed in an essential war industry. One must not forget .that our district is not like an entirely urban district. On the contrary, the Quebec division might be said to be an essentially rural one, which explains that many potential recruits are momentarily exempted from compulsory military training. One must, however, emphasize the fact that these men have complied with the law and have been granted regular exemptions.
I was anxious, Mr. Chairman, to make this correction to-night so that the falsehoods published yesterday in the English language newspapers might be rectified to-morrow.
Progress reported.
